(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I wish to rise to a question of privilege relating to a letter written by Dr. Nadeau, medical officer of the immigration branch at Quebec, which I will read before the House because he apparently so desires. Dr. Nadeau is under the impression that in the remarks which I offered the other day upon the question of 1 immigration I did cast insinuations upon

the integrity of the medical men of Quebec who are immigration officers. Here is what he writes to me:
Quebec, April 21, 1908. My dear Lavergne,-My attention has just been called to a report which ' I/Aetion Sociale ' of the 18th instant has given of a speech purpoted to have been lately delivered by yon in the House upon the question of immigration.
Following is the report of ' L'Action Sociale:'

I challenge the minister, said Mr. Lavergne, to have an inquiry made into the Salvation Army and the immigrants it has brought into Quebec, and to ask the doctors at Quebec to give their evidence; but I hope this time the government will not stop the mouths of the witnesses who give evidence. There has been collusion between the officers at Quebec and the Salvation Army and I have it from officers who receive the immigrants at Quebec that before they pass the medical examination these immigrants go to the barracks and get the password of the Salvation Army at Quebec, and then go back and answer the doctor. The minister cannot contradict that, if he looks at the correspondence produced.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member is making a great many statements which he puts forward as statements of fact. The statement that immigrants coming out under the auspices of the Salvation Army are treated any different from any other immigrants who come out, so far as my knowledge goes, is absolutely incorrect; and if he can by any means demonstrate that it is the fact we will have a change in the immigration service at Quebec immediately.

All last summer the immigrants brought out by the Salvation Army were sent to the barracks and there they got the password from the Salvation Army officers to answer the doctors of the Immigration Department. Not only was a complaint laid before the Interior Department here, but Mr. Doyle and the immigration doctors at Quebec, I think Dr. Nadeau and Dr. Potvin were advised, that if there were one hundred Salvation Army immigrants, they would pass before the doctor first, but if less, they would go to the barracks first. That is the statement I have to make and on it I would like the department to throw more light.
Dr. Nadeau adds:
So then, the Salvation Army of England, exclusively, devotes its attention in the recruiting of immigrants, without trying to locate them, relying as to that upon its representatives at Quebec, whose business office is under the same roof as the office of the government agent himself, where all examinations are passed, medical and civil.
As a rule, those representatives keep a list of employment offers to several mechanics or to farmers far in excess of the number of arrivals. Thus thev are able to direct sys-tematicallv and more safely these people to their destination.
The immigrants who do not come under the Mr. A. LAVERGNE
auspices of the Salvation Army are supposed to have received at the time of their departure from Europe the necessary directions that will enable them to reach their destination ; at least, that is mentioned on their tickets. So that they can go directly from the medical inspectors to the civil inspectors, who require them to say what trade or calling thev follow, and where they are going.
At first, immigrants coming out under the auspices of the Salvation Army, having passed the medicad examination, had to go to the barracks to learn what their destination was and then came back to comply with all the requirements of the civil examination.
That system gave rise to many inconven-iencies, above all it greatlv delayed the inspection. It was then decided that the immigrants would go to the barracks first in order to learn what their destination is and should afterwards pass the medical examination, so as to be able to give all the necessary information, when passing the civil examination.
This rule was to apply only if there were less than one hundred Salvation Army immigrants. Otherwise, the Salvation Army officers, for convenience sake, volunteered to attend at the arrival of the steamer at Rimouski, in order to acquaint all the passengers with their destination, so that everything should be ready when they landed at Quebec.
Neither Mr. Doyle or the doctors did ever receive from Ottawa any directions as to that; but the representative of the Salvation Army the immigration agent and the doctors came to an understanding. Besides, all those particulars of the administration are settled in the same way. Our instructions concerning the medical examination of the immigrants admit of no relaxation in favour of anybody, neither for the Salvation Army people nor for any other immigrants. Moreover, I am at a loss to understand what password could be given to the diseased immigrants, so as to conceal their shortcomings, when they come to pass the medical examination.
Dr. Nadeau's letter shows that what I stated the other day is entirely true, namely, that the immigrants who come out under the auspices of the Salvation Army are treated differently from other immigrants. The officers of the Interior Department at Quebec confer with the representatives of the Salvation Army. I said nothing else.
I never intended to cast any reflection upon the integrity of the medical officers at the port of Quebec. I am satisfied that they all discharge their duty. This I did say and I say again : the immigrants that come out under the auspices of the Salvation Army receive a different treatment; the officers of the Army that take care of those immigrants are located in the same building as the immigration agency. When they come out, they do not know where to go, having all been inscribed by their officers as farm labourers: then the representatives of the Army direct them where to go, and as the majority of them are mechanics they do not go out and work upon farms, not-

withstanding the policy of the government, as laid down by the minister.

Mr. Speaker,
I have received from Mr. Parent, the Chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission, the following papers, which I desire to lay before the House :
The Commissioners of the Transcontinental Railway, Ottawa.	.
Office of the Chairman,
April 23, 1908.
Memorandum to the R;t. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Prime Minister.
A letter from Major Hodgins, lately our district engineer, at Kenora, Ontario, has been given wide publicity in the press, namely by the Manitoba ' Free Press' and the Ottawa ' Morning Citizen,' where it was commented upon.	.
There are insinuations and statements in it that should not be allowed to pass unanswered.	,
Without laying anv specific charges, Mr. Hodgins makes vague, general accusations that are absolutely groundless. It is plain that the object in view is to cause us annoyance, without any regard to truth or public interest	[DOT]
If Major Hodgins has had in his possession anv evidence of irregularities or wrong-doing, he should have submitted such to the commissioners. As a corporate body, and being the first concerned, it would have been our dutv to investigate the matter promptly, rl he'had done so. and the commissioners had refused to look into his charges, then he might have be.en justified m issuing statements to the public. There is nothing in Major Hodgins* allegations to indicate that he is even now in possession of any such evidence.	.	.
Taking up seriatim the allegations m Major Hodgins' letter as printed m the
^l^That the government is paying padded accounts for the work done, and that the Grand Trunk Pacific people are making no objection because they merely have to pay the added interest.	,
This statement is without any fondation. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company make objections when they see fit, and these are looked into at once with due care.
2.	They (the commissioners) wanted to change iny ideas, based on a good many years experience, on the construction to the classification that is allowed to contractors in
^This statement is also without foundation. The commissioners never, at any time, requested Major Hodgins to adopt in his district any classification not in accordance with the contract and specifications. As to the classification in Quebec, it was looked over and found to be agreeing with these and therefore perfectly regular.
3.	If Mr. Poulin, the engineer appointed by Mr. Parent to replace me on the western district. has allowed the introduction of a classification similar to that allowed in Quebec, this will account for the increase in the estimated cost of the line. If this increase
amounts to $3,000,000 or $1,000,000 it is time the public demanded some explanation.
Such hypothetical statements of course amount to nothing at all. In the first place, Mr. Poulin was not appointed by Mr. Parent, the chairman, who did not even suggest it, but by the 'board, on the recommendation of the chief engineer, because he was considered to be the best rran for the position and to take hold of th< work of organizing the district, which had been left in such a had shape by Major Hodgins. At this point it may be well to remark that classification comes from the chief engineer and not the chairman or the commissioners as Major Hodgins puts it.
Since leaving our employment, Major Hodgins has talked a good deal openly, m fact much more than professional dignity and the sense of justice would seem usuallv to permit.
It is time, we feel, in justice to ourselves and to the public, before whom there is an evident desire to misrepresent the facts, to call a halt and make it necessary for the accuser to bring facts to substantiate his charges.
You will find, attached, newspaper clippings in reference to Major Hodgins' letter, and all correspondence relating to the circumstances of his dismissal; also a letter from our chief engineer, Mr. Lumsden, on the same subject.
In conclusion the commissioners would respectfully request, as they do not wish to remain under the aspersion which such reports cast oil them, that the whole matter be referred to and looked into by a committee ot the House, and that Major Hodgins be assigned to appear before the same to repeat his charges in a specific manner in order to substantiate them if he can. Then an opportunity will be given right minded people to see where the truth is and if public interest would have'been better served by keeping an engineer who ignored the specifications or by replacing him, as was done, by one who will follow them.	,
The commissioners trust their request will receive early attention.

Chairman.
The communication of the chief engineer referred to in this letter Is as follows :
Ottawa, April 23, 1908. Sirs,-In regard to the article which appeared in the Manitoba Free Press of the 18tb instant and the editorial in the Morn ing Citizen' of the 22nd instant referring to a letter from Major E. A. Hodgins, now of Victoria, B.C., I beg to state that as far as I know no estimates or accounts for work done have been padded. The Grand Trunk Pacific have made from time to time some general objections as to classifications m dlstrmt 1 >
but until after the dates above referred to no details giving actual points where such over-classification was claimed were submitted to me. As you are aware I on the 11th and 30th January, issued special circulars to the district engineers, giving my interpretation of clauses 34, 35 and 36 of our general specifications accompanied by a diagram explanatory of same, and I have letters from the district engineers in districts A, B, and F where actual grading was being proceeded with, stating that my interpretation had been and is being adhered to. My letter of the 19th of September last to the chairman, gives

my reasons for suggesting a change in district engineers in district F.
Your obedient servant,
_	.	HUGH LUMSDEN.
*the Commissioners of the Transcontinental Railway,
Ottawa, Ont.
In view of the request contained in this letter, I beg to inform my hon. friend and the House that on Monday next I will move that the matter be referred to a special committee for investigation.

I beg to renew my question of yesterday as to whether a report has been made by Mr. Gaudet who has conducted the Sorel investigation and to ask the minister to bring the report down to the House if it is ready ?
Mr. Gaudet came to Ottawa the other day to complete the investigation. I hope the report will be ready for Monday.

Has the Finance Minister any information to give us with respect to the Insurance Bill which was brought down some weeks ago ? It was the subject of more or less investigation in the Banking and Commerce Committee, but since that time little has been heard of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In view of the very extended hearing which took place before the Committee on Banking and Commerce and the numerous statements made, I desired that some time should elapse before proceeding with the Bill, in order that the officials of the Insurance Department might have an opportunity of studying all that was said. We hope at an early date to make a further move in the matter.
Has the Minister of Railways any further information in regard to the printing of the report of the Quebec Bridge Commission ?

I made inquiry concerning that report, and I believe that the report proper with the appendices will be printed in a very short time. The drawings and the other parts of the report will be a little later.
I might say in this connection that I propose to move at the proper time that more than the ordinary number of copies shall be printed on account of the very many inquiries we have had for the report. We have had several cables from Europe, and the High Commissioner has informed us that he has had a great manv inquiries. In order to supply that demand which I

think we should do for the general information of the public, we will have to send quite a large number there. It strikes me that it would be very proper that at least one or two copies of the report should be placed in each public library and that every university library ought to have two or three copies for general information.

FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

Before you -leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on two or three subjects I understood last night that the order of business to-day would be Supply, the estimates of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-

ley) being taken up. I see that bon. gentleman is not in his place ; and, as in a few minutes, I wish to address a few remarks to him, I will thank the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurler) if he will ask the Minister of Public Works to be in his seat. Meantime, I will occupy a few minutes with another matter.
I am not at all surprised that the government, after having a number of scandals exposed during the present session in connection with timber limits, mining leases, civil service administration, dredging contracts and numerous other matters, have sent the rank and file of their supDorters hunting through the files of the departments covering the term of the Conservative administration for material to offset these scandals, if possible. We have many instances here in recent discussions of lion, gentlemen referring to matters which they could only find in the files of the departments. It is evident that a horde has been sent hunting through the files containing the records under the Conservative government to see if something could not be raked up reflecting upon the action of Conservative members of this House. A few days ago. an hon. gentleman was put up to make charges against myself. This hon. gentleman said :
I also find another member of this parliament who is known to most of you, Geo. Tay-' lo'' M.P.. who made application for friends for townships 39. 40 and 41, ranges 18, 19 and 20 west meridian, not a very small application ; he did not go in for small things.
Hear, hear.
I immediately rose in my place and said :

If the hon. gentleman will allow me-he has been perusing the records, I presume, of the Department of the Interior, where he gets his information. I challenge him to produce an aoplic'ation signed bv me on behalf of anybody. Mr. Walter Beatv made an application in his own behalf, and I tol'wa rdi (1 his letter. The hon. gentleman cannot find anything else in the department, no application that I ever made, either on my own behalf or on behalf of anybody else. He has made a statement. I challenge him either to produce the proof or to withdraw the statement.
The hon. gentleman is like the rest, he says he made an application, and gives the name of one.
No, I did not make an application ; I inclosed his letter in one I wrote to the minister.
That is just as good.

Is that a crime? It is sim-plv disgraceful for a member to get up in his place and make a charge against a mem-be" of narliament, and then either refuse to ta_ke it hack or to produce the document.
And further on :
The hon. gentleman said that the applications are on file; are they in the department or in the library?
I said the records were in the library.
Where?
In the ' Hansard.'
In the speech made by the late Ananias Cameron?

And John Charlton.
Mr. TAY'LOR. Thev made statements, as the hon. "-entleman is making them, without anv authority
I repeat that challenge to-day-let the government search every file during the administration of the late Conservative government, and they will not find an application made by me, either on my own behalf or on behalf of anybody else for any timber limit. I happened to be in the Public Accounts Committee and was looking over one of the files that had been brought to the committee in charge of an officer of one of the departments-for members of the opposition have no rights, we are told, and a government officer was in charge of the file. I looked over it and made a precis of what the file contained. Here is a portion of it:
Lettex- dated Seixtember 2, 1903, from Latch-ford, McDongall & Daly, applying on behalf of Colin & Campbell, of Edmonton, to have department advertise a timber berth in the district of Alberta, 8 miles by 31 miles on each side of McLeod river. Berth was numbered 1096.
September 10, 1903. Letter from P. G. Iteves to Latchfoi'd, McDougall & Daly, informing them that berth 1096 should be shortly advertised.
Letter dated September JO. P. G. Keyes to Crown timber agent of Edmonton, informing him to the same effect.
September 10, letter from P. G. Keyes to E. Stewart, Department of Forestry, Ottawa, inclosing copy of advertisement for berth 1096 in district of Alberta.
There are a lot of other letters on file that do not amount to much, but after a while we come down to a letter dated Ottawa, November 11. 1903, as follows :
I hereby offer a bonus of $1,000 for timber berth No. 1096 containing "	square
miles, situated	for which public
competition is being invited, and I inclose an accepted cheque on Traders' Bank for $1,000, being amount of said bonus.
(Sgd.) JOHN GENTLES,
Kincardine, Per J. T.
On the margin is marked ' received cheque $1,000, 11-11-03.'
(Sgd.) P. R, for accountant.
This letter is marked as having been received, stamped with the Department of the Interior, Wednesday- 18th November, 1903, Timber and Mines Branch.
On the bottom of the letter is written in red ink to address letter to Hon. John Tolmie, Kincardine, Ontario.
This tender was I'eceived in an envelope bearing no post-mark, the address printed thereon being ' Timber and Mines Branch, Department of the Interior. Ottawa.'
There is no stamp on envelope as to when it was received.

Memo, attached: John Gentles, care of Hon. John Tolmie, Kincardine, Ontario.
Cash $1,000 bonus for license to cut timber on limit 1096.
And here is copy of a receipt dated November 11, Department of the Interior, Timber and Mines Branch :

Then there is more correspondence involving a good deal of dickering, but I need not quote any of it until we come to a letter dated Kincardine, 11th February, 1904, and addressed to P. G. Keyes, secretary :
My Dear Sir,-Inclosed please find license duly signed by Mr. Gentles and returned by mvself. There is something I do not fully understand, and that is that while the license states the lease is from December 11, 1903, to April 30, 1901. the receipt for moneys paid states from December 11, 1903, to December 11, 1904. Kindly explain this.
Yours truly,
(Sg3.) JOHN TOLMIE.
Then there is correspondence showing that the ground rent had not been paid. Mr. Keyes writes to Mr. Tolmie stating that amounts owing on berths 1092, 1095 and 1096 had been called to his attention on 28th September, and if they were not paid within thirty days steps would be taken to have berths cancelled, and he now begs to state that the amount involved had not been paid, and that Mr. Gentles' right to cut timber on these berths was withdrawn from the records of the department. Mr. Tolmie wrote back immediately under date of November 20, 1905, as follows :-
Hon. Frank Oliver,
Minister of the Interior.
Dear Mr. Oliver,-I inclose you a letter from the secretary of vour department which explains itself. My partner, Mr. John Gentles, in this deal

Mr. Gentles was his partner in this deal. It looks as if he had had a good many other deals.
My partner, Mr. John Gentles, in this deal was inclined to throw up and hence the delay in paving the ground rent. Kindly send me statement of account due with interest to date and wa will send it to you on receipt of the statement.
Kindest regards from yours truly,

Mr. Tolmie was a member then, because there were several letters addressed to him in the House of Commons when the correspondence was going on. I need not read all the letters, but there is another one here dated 16th June, 1906.
W. W. Cory,
Deputy Minister of the Interior.
Dear Mr. Cory,-As I told you the other day by phone we sold the limits owned by Mr. TAYLOR.
Mr. Gentles and myself, 1092, 1095 and 1096, on the McLeod river, Alberta. The ground rent has been paid by us until either the 1st of Mav or 1st of June, 1906. The parties purchasing the same assume the payment of the rent for 1906-7. The assignment from Mr. Gentles, signed bv him, has been mailed to you, and I trust the non-payment of rent by us for 1906-7 will not be a bar in the way of closing the assignment as we have lost enough. The party purchasing them has inspected the limits and are satisfied, and I trust you will complete vour part with us with as much despatch as possible.
Then comes the assignment of these limits to Mr. Gentles at $4,000. These are copies of the original documents on file, showing that a member of this House, while he was a member, made application with his partner Mr. Gentles, and got a limit from this government and sold the same for $4,000. Yet in the face of facts such as these, hon. gentlemen in the back benches will get up and accuse hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who .never had anything to do with limits, in order to throw out to the country that we were as bad or worse when the Conservatives were in power. That is all I propose saying on that matter.
Now I have another matter with regard to which I wish to say a few words with regard to the Minister of Public Works. Two days ago when my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) moved the adjournment of the House in order to discuss an important matter-and it has turned out to be important, because since that discussion the Minister of Public Works has cancelled the order in council that he had passed renewing certain dredging contracts. When the matter was up I undertook to discuss a question relating to the Quebec harbour improvement in which there was some dredging, and the Minister of Public Works raised a point of order that I could not discuss that matter because the motion only referred to dredging contracts in the neighbourhood of Midland. But in reading the resolution, you, Mr. Speaker, said it read ' there and at other points ' and you authorized me to speak on dredging elsewhere. Then I referred to a contract that was given by this government and notified the Minister of Public Works not to renew it again. It was given in 1903 for the Quebec harbour improvements, in which there was a large amount of dredging done, but with the dredging there were certain goods supplied. That contract has been extended from year to year up to last year. There was paid on the first contract, No. 4613, $183,000. Then it was extended by order in council and a new contract. No. 5111, was made, on which $224,000 was paid. That was renewed by another order in council, and on the new contract, No. 5693. $107,000 were paid. Then it was renewed again by another order In council, a new contract was made. No. 5888, on 1 which there were paid $98,000. A total of

$614,000 was paid in four years for the harbour improvements in Quebec. A contract was given to a firm by the name of Dussault and Lemieux. I presume they may have had it extended, I do not know whether there has been an order in council extending it to this year or not. But I drew the attention of the House to the fact that according to my information, which I believe is correct, a contract for dredging was given at 75 cents a yard, and the gentleman who got this contract had neither dredge nor anything else to do the work with, and they farmed it out for 15 cents a yard to other contractors, and pocketed 60 cents clear for themselves on this job-More than that, they had clearing work to do. This dredge that was getting 75 cents a yard dumped the material over into the dock and then got 32 cents a yard for the filling. This is my information, and I believe it is correct.
Would the hon. gentleman tell me to whom they farmed it out ?
We will likely have an inquiry, and we will get the particulars, but I am anxious that another order in council should not be passed extending the time.
Would it not be more convenient to discuss it when we have the inquiry ?

My hon. friend might pass an order in council extending the contract, and rob the country for another year. It is to prevent that taking place that I bring up this discussion now, and to notify him that this contract must not be extended another year. Now among the items charged for there are drift bolts, iron, 105,600 pounds at 7 cents a pound. Any person who has ever built a dock knows that drift bolts are simply a bar of iron cut in lengths of 10, 16, 18 or 24 inches long, pointed or sharpened, and anybody knows that you can bjty iron at $1.00 or $1.75 per 100 pounds. Yet these gentlemen have been paying from year to year 7 cents a pound for these drift bolts. I took the trouble to write to a party to know what he would furnish them for, and this is what he answered :
I have your favour of the 19th and am much obliged. Bolts such as you ask about including drift bolts nointed at one end are worth about 3 cents ner pound. It would depend altogether upon the nature of the specification and how badly we wanted the order, but you could figure two and three-quarter cents per pound as a minimum and about 3J cents per pound as maximum. This would be f.o.b. factory.
Having a nut on one end would not affect the price hardly at all. as these large nuts are sold almost at the same price as bolts.
They get 8 cents a pound for screw bolts, iron. A screw bolt is simply a steel plate with a hole punched in it, and anybody can
buy them for 2 cents a pound. Then we find stone ballast in cribs, 10,500 cubic yards at $1.25. Dredging foundation, 18,000 cubic yards at 75 cents a yard. This is being farmed out at 15 cents a yard. Then stone and gravel foundation, 4,490 cubic yards, at $2.50. Earth filling, 60,400 cubic yards at 32 cents. This was lifted up by the dredge at 75 cents and dumped in at 32 cents more.

The hon. gentleman characterizes the price as extremely high for the drift bolts. Would he be surprised to know that Mackenzie and Mann are paying me to-day 7 cents a pound for drift bolts, and the prices are put down by themselves in cases where I had no special price mentioned and the quantities are much larger than he has quoted.
If the hon. gentleman wants to make a good profit, I will supply them at 2f cents and ship them from the factory.
I can buy just as cheaply as the hon. gentleman.

My word is as good as the hon. gentleman's. I will supply the bolts at 21 cents. I will get a man who will take the contract for supplying the bolts to Mackenzie and Mann at 2\ cents.
Mr. .1. T. SCHELL. Does he mean the bolts with the nuts on?
Yes. They say they make no difference between the drift bolts pointed without the nuts and with the nuts on.
I will take a contract at that rate.
Then I will give it to you.
Nothing smaller than three-quarters of an inch.
We will discuss that afterwards. Any statement I make here, I am prepared to carry out. The hon. Minister of Public Works attempted to bluff-
To what? Do I hear the hon. gentleman right?

Yes. You undertook to bluff me the other day. If that expression is not parliamentary, Mr. Speaker, I am willing to withdraw it, but I want the minister to understand that as regards being conversant with the practice of this parliament, he is a mere fledgeling and is losing his time when he attempts to practice on old parliamentarians what perhaps he had the privilege of doing in New Brunswick.
Do not stir up his feelings.

I have always thought, and the people have a perfect right to think,

that when an hon. minister makes a statement in parliament, that statement should be true as the gospel. But when he makes a statement that is not in accord with the facts, how much confidence can the people place in him? Here is the statement I made the other day:
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works, if he has yet completed the return in reference to Petit Rocher ?

On making inquiry of my deputy, I find that the answer given contained exactly the information which was asked for, that is, matters detailed on a certain page of the Auditor General's report. If any hon. friend desires further information and will be good enough to put another question, I shall be glad to give him the further information.
It was not a question at all but a motion for.a return.

It was for a return as to
matters detailed on a certain page of the Auditor General's Report, and that return has been made and is complete.
There Is the minister's reply.
Hear, hear.
And he puts the onus on his deputy. I am acquainted with his deputy, and I am satisfied that his deputy would not put in anybody's mouth a statement not in accord with the facts.
Hear, hear.

That statement must have come directly from the minister. Now what are the facts ? Here is the motion I made for that return, and in that motion there is not a word making any reference at all to the Auditor General's Report. Yet the minister says that my motion had reference to matter contained in that report.
Would the hon. gentleman kindly read it?

I read it before and the minister went away and came back and tried to bluff me the second time. I shall read it now and ask the hon. gentleman to make an apology:
Return to an address of the House of Com-rnons, dated the 15th January, 1908, for a copy of all correspondence, telegrams, orders in council, contracts and tenders, with the names and amount of each, in possession of the government or any member or official thereof, respecting the construction of a breakwater at Petit Rocher, on the southwestern side of Bale des Chaleurs, as detailed on page 74 of the report of the Minister of Public Works, tor the year ended 31st March, 1907.
Quite so.

Is there anything in that about the Auditor General's Report? That refers to page 74 of the minister's own report. Yet he comes here and will not give me the answer but tells me something that Mr. TAYLOR.
is possibly untrue. Here is the report. What does it say?
Petit Rocher is a farming, fishing and lumbering settlement on the southwestern side of Baie des Chaleurs, twelve miles north of Bathurst.
To afford protection to the fishing boats and vessels trading in Baie des Chaleurs, for which there is no natural shelter in the vicinity, and to facilitate the shipment of lumber, a contract was entered into May 31, 1904, with Simon McGregor, for the construction of a breakwater, consisting of a main work, 209 feet long on the outer face, and a wing or ' L,' placed at an angle of 74 degrees 30 minutes with the main part, 160 feet long on the outer face. The width on top will be 30 feet. At its inner end the breakwater will be 480 feet from the shore. The depth along the inner face varies from 11 to 18J feet at low water.
In 1904-5, a right of way, 860 feet long, from the public road to the shore was opened up, graded and fenced.
The contract work was begun on March 18, 1905, and by the end of 1904-5 two cribs, 96J and 41 feet long respectively, had been built and sunk in place.
A crib to form the remainder of the work was started on February 19, 1906, but on March 11, when it had reached a height of about six tiers, it was carried away by' the ice. It was, however, recovered on May 14. The outer section, which was intended to complete the main part of the breakwater was found to be intact and work on it was resumed. By the end of the fiscal year this crib had been built to a height of nineteen tiers and the two cribs sunk in 1905 had been filled with ballast and built up to half tide level, and the upper ballast floors were laid.
During the fiscal year 1906-7, the crib forming the remainder of the main work was sunk in place and a crib to complete the ' L ' was begun and placed in position. The building of the superstructure was continued on the main part up to about high water level, when two storms, on November 12 and 16 carried away nearly the whole top, the break being about 9 feet in extreme depth.
Work was resumed on March 7, and by the close of the fiscal year the remains of three damaged tiers of face timbers had been removed, and a part of the wrecked superstructure near the southern end rebuilt, the interior being filled with ballast.
The expenditure for the fiscal year 1906-7 was $5,029.60.
That is what I wanted the Information for.

It seems a pity to take up the time of the House discussing whether or not a certain return Is according to the motion calling for it. My hon. friend says he has the most perfect confidence in my deputy. I may repeat to him that the instructions sent to my deputy were to furnish a complete answer to the motion made by my hon. friend, and the return laid on the table was made by the deputy. If the hon. gentleman doubts my statement, he is at perfect liberty to communicate himself, either in writing or verbally, with the de-
APEtL 24, 1908
puty, and my deputy will confirm what I have said. If there be any omission, it rests with the deputy, and the deputy informed me that he had made a complete return as required by the motion.

After my having read the motion for the return and pointing out that the return simply comes down to 1905 and does not refer to the carrying away of the piers, as detailed in page 74 of the minister's report, referred to in the motion for the return, or the expenditure since, or who the contractor was or how the contract was let, the hon. gentleman still insists that it is a complete return. But is it not evident that the return is not complete, and that the minister's statement the other day was not in accord with the facts?

I called the attention of the deputy to the page to which my hon. friend refers, and the deputy still asserted that he had sent a complete return of all the correspondence which there had been upon the subject as detailed upon that page of the report. It was the report of the Minister of Public Works. It is a misquotation when the Auditor General's Report is mentioned. It was the report mentioned in the motion of my hon. friend which was referred to the deputy and his return is based upon that. When I called his attention to it he assured me that he had sent a complete return of everything in the department on the subject.

Then the minister had better go back to the department and give his deputy a lecture for putting in his mouth a statement which is not correct When I brought it up upon the first occasion I got the same answer. I brought it up again and I was put down; I could not proceed to discuss it.
I must take the statement of my deputy.
I have not received the information as yet, and I want the return completed. The return brought down only goes to 1905 and the expenditure is in 1906-7.
If the hon. gentleman will put the matter in the form of a question I will see that he will get a complete answer.
I will put no more questions until the return is completed or until the minister complies with the order of the House. The minister must obey that order and complete that return.
All I can say to my hon. friend is that I can do no more than I have done.
Then the minister had better resign his position.
One moment

I am making my speech, and when I get through the minister may get up and answer me. All he can do is to come here and tell us that the deputy has told him he has complied with the return, that he can do no more when, on the face of it, he must know and admit before the House that the return is not complete and that he made a statement the other day which is not in accordance with the facts.
I do not know it, I do not admit it, and I shall believe my deputy until I learn the contrary.

I would believe the deputy, too, much sooner than I would believe the minister in view of the statement which he made in the House the other day I have as much confidence in the deputy as the hon. gentleman has, because I knew him long before the minister did. I can tell the hon. gentleman that hon. members on this side of the House are not going to be bluffed down by him saying that is the only return, or that is all you can get unless you put another motion or ask another question. I am not going to put another motion and I am not going to ask another question ; I am going to ask the minister to comply with the order of the House and complete that return.

I might give an explanation to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor), who has just taken his seat, in reference to a portion of the work at Petit Rocker. The contractor is the master of his own work, and if, through inexperience, he makes mistakes he is responsible for them and has to account to the department for them. A portion of this work, in the spring of 3906. was carried away by the ice. The tide is very strong in that locality and the ice carried away the work. He was responsible for it and had to pay for it. He had to do his work over again, and naturally nothing would appear in the accounts of the engineer or of the department. The contractor had to make good the loss and that should explain the lack in the report of the department.
Then the hon. gentleman (Mr. Turgeou) admits that the return whicli has been brought down is not complete?
It is complete in so far as the department is concerned. The contractor paid $4,000 or $5,000 twice, but that was his own loss and the department has not lost one dollar by it.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Public Works-chargeable to income-Nova Scotia-Antigonish, public building, $7,000.
This amount is required to complete the new building which is in course of construction at Antigonish.
What kind of a building is it?
A public building, brick with stone foundation, 33 x 35, 2t storeys high.
What is it to be used for ?
Post office, customs house and office of the resident engineer of the Public Works Department.
Is there much busi ness done at that point?
It is quite a thriving town.
Is it a port of entry:
Yes.
How much will the building cost?
$28,700, which will include the cost of the building, heating, plumbing, wiring, fixtures, furniture, &c.
How much did the land cost and from whom was it purchased?
I have not the memorandum here ; the cost of the site is not given.
When was that building commenced?
It was begun in 1905.
Whom was the site bought from and how much did it cost?
I find that the site was owned by the Crown, so that we had nothing to pay for it.
Who is the architect?
Mr. Ewart, the Chief Architect of the department. The plans were prepared in the department under the direction of the Chief Architect.
Shall we have any more to vote after this, or is this the end of it?
No, nothing more to vote; this is the end of it.
Was there any outside architect employed to make these plans?
No outside architect.
I think the hon. minister stated that the plans for public buildings were mostly all made in the department.
Yes, plans for post offices, custom houses and buildings of that kind are in the great majority of cases made in the department.
Is there a superintendent of the work during construction?

Yes, there is a clerk of
works-.
Who is he, and what is his salary?
His name is Mr. Mc-Gillivray, and ne received $3 per day.
What was the total payment to the clerk of works?
I cannot at this moment tell my hon. friend, but he received $3 per day.
For the four years during wnich the buildings has been under construction?
Simply while the work of construction has been going on.

Has not this building been under construction for many years? I remember that the first vote for it was taken when the gentleman who is now a member of the Transcontinental Railway-Commission was a member of this House for the county of Antigonish.
The contract was let in 1905. That would be something over two years.
Was the clerk of the works paid for all that time?
I presume he would be paid for the time he attended the work.
Why would this building require three years to complete?
It is quite an expensive building-a $28,000 building.
It should be built in four or five months.
I may say that the contractors are very excellent people-Rhodes, Curry & Co.-and would not take longer than was necessary.
Would the hon. minister say that a building that would cost $28,000 would not be unduly delayed if it took two years to complete it?

It would not necessarily follow that it was unduly delayed. The contract was not let until the summer of 1905, and it would not be many months until the winter was on, when building operations would cease.

At what time was the contract let?
Mr. PUGSREY'. Not until June.

There would be ample time, then, to have the outside walls erected before the winter. I have done a considerable amount of building myself, and have built up to Christmas in the climate of New Brunswick, which is not very much less severe than that of Nova Scotia, and I do-

not think there would be any difficulty at all about completing the outside walls of this building by the time building operations would have to cease for the winter. The inside work would certainly be done in the winter time. Have you no memorandum of what the inspection of this building cost? -because sometimes the cost of inspection bears a very large proportion to the cost of the work.

1 may say to my hon. friend that the expenditure under the head of incidental expenses was $1,938, which would include the salary of the clerk of works, and I presume also advertising, printing, and the like of that. If my hon. friend wants to know exactly what was paid to the clerk of works, I can get it.
Yes. What is Mr. Mc-Gillivray's occupation?
I have not his occupation. His name is A. McGillivray.
It would not follow that he would be a builder at all.
I should be glad to get the information for my hon. friend.
He might be a tailor, you know.
Sometimes tailors are men of very good judgment.
Very good iudgment indeed, in the cut of a suit of clothes, but not necessarily in the quality of work on a building.
I know that my hon. friend would think, although he is a lawyer, that he knows a good deal about building.
Because I have built a good many buildings.
Was the work let by tender and given to the lowest tenderer?
Let by tender. Three tenders were received in answer to public advertisement, and Rhodes, Curry & Co. were the lowest and received the contract.
What was the amount of the tenders?
They ranged from $14,990 to $19,898.
What did these tenders cover?
I will tell my hon. friend what they did not cover-the heating, the wiring, the town clock, the fittings.
How much would it cost for the heating?
Who had that contract?
Rhodes, Curry & Co.
What was the cost Of the wiring?
Do I understand the minister to say that it cost $650 to wire the building for electric lights?
Not only to put the wiring in, but also for the fittings and electroliers.
Did Rhodes, Curry & Co. get the contract at that tender of $14,990?
Yes.
How much have they received altogether?
I could not tell my hon. friend what has been paid to Rhodes, Curry & Co., but the total amount paid to the 31st of October, 1907, was $21,323.
Did the contractors do the work for the price tendered or were they paid extras ?
They did not receive any extras. They were paid $14,990, the amount of the contract.
The hon. minister has already paid out $21,000 and is asking for more. He cites one contract for $14,990. Will he give the other contracts for the extra expenditure ?
Printing and advertising, clerk of the works salary, &c., $2,024.90.
I would like to have the separate items.
I should be very glad indeed to get them for my hon. friend but 1 cannot have them this afternoon.
Better let that item stand.
Does my hon. friend not think he should allow that to pass, on the understanding that I will furnish the information on some other item ?
The trouble is you never furnish it but always forget.
I will undertake to furnish it.
Go on and give the items.
Printing and advertising and clerk of the works salary, &c.~ $2,024.90 ; paid to the contractor up to 31st of October, 1907, $14,990. That is the price of the contract. For a boiler, $229.80.
From whom was that bought ?
I do not know, the price is not very high.
It depends on the kind of boiler.
Tower clock $1,140.
From whom was that bought ?
From R. D. Kirk. There were tenders called for.
Is it the custom of the department to put up clocks on all the buildings ?

Not in all of them, but in towns of some considerable importance the department has very frequently put up clocks in the towers. Sometimes the tower is built suitable for a clock. Some twenty years ago a building was erected by the government and the holes were made in the tower for a clock. A few weeks ago I had a delegation urging most strongly that I should supply the clock which should have been supplied twenty years ago.
I hope you will do it.
I intend to.
Are you going to put up a clock in the Yalleyfleld post office ?
If my hon. friend will make representations on the subject, I will consider the matter.
Well, I make the application now.
How about the post office at Sussex ? Is there a clock there ?
Is there a tower provided for the clock ?
Yes, there is an opportunity to put a clock there.
If there is any provision made for a clock, 1 will consider the matter. That building was erected fifteen years ago, did the hon. gentleman ever urge very strongly that a clock should be put there ?

I did not suppose it was the policy of the government to distribute these clocks. But now that the government are so generous, I thought it would be quite in accord with the policy of the minister and his love for that constituency which he used to represent, that he would undertake to do something for it. It is certainly ns important as Antigouish.
I hope the hon. gentleman will not try to prevent this being done for Antigonish.
It is done already so that I could not prevent it even if I wanted to.
Tower clock, $1,140 ; sidewalk, &c., $735.30.
Is that sidewalk just in from off the building?
It is' the paving all around the public building.
What material ?
I presume granolithic.
How many square feet ?
The size of the lot is 240 square yards and my hon. friend can figure that out for himself.
You cannot figure from that. I do not know how wide the sidewalk is and how many square feet in it.
It is a corner lot.
How many square feet around the lot? Is the sidewalk three feet or six feet wide ?
I have not that information, I am sorry to say.
Is the sidewalk on four streets or on two streets ?
On two streets.

That is a pretty good price.
Mr. PUGSLEY! I think that a granolithic, fairly wide sidewalk would probably cost that much.
What is the size of the building ?
Thirty-three feet by fifty-five with an annex twelve by thirty-three.
The annex would not be on both streets. There would be no sidewalk for the annex.
The sidewalk would be on both streets.
You can only figure 33 feet one way and 55 the other ?
I take it for granted the government would build a sidewalk around the whole lot.
They would go to the line of their lot. Is the lot 55 feet each way ?
The only information I have here with regard to the lot is that it contains 240 square yards.

At $700 you would be paying two prices, but that is not sufficiently unusual to be remarkable.
Mr. PUGSLEY". I forgive my hon. friend that statement because if he did not make it, he would not be acting in accordance with his usual practice. He often indulges in these statements but perhaps thoughtlessly.
Mr. FOWLER, The minister knows me better than that.
Is it not usual for the town or city to pay some proportion of the cost of the sidewalk or does the government put a sidewalk all around the lot?
The chief architect informs me that where the government erects a building and a sidewalk has to be built, the government usually pays the whole cost.
The sidewalk around the post office in the town of Truro is in very bad condition. I would like the government to put that sidewalk in good order, if it is their business to do that.
That would be repairing the sidewalk. No doubt if the town made representations to the department, they would be received with a desire to contribute something, probably pay half the cost.
At the public building in Sussex there is no sidewalk laid down by the government at all. I would suggest that the government put a sidewalk there.
Is there a sidewalk on each side of the building ?
There is a street but no granolithic sidewalk.
In cases where the town has built a granolithic sidewalk along a public building
But the town has not.

I presume that the sidewalk in front of the public building in Sussex is the same as the sidewalk on the street above and below. It would be somewhat anomalous to have a different sidewalk In front of one building from that in front of the buildings on either side.
Not necessarily?
If your lot is 60 feet front by 120 feet deep, which is a large sized lot for a town, as in most towns they are 40 feet front by 80 feet, and supposing the sidewalk is six feet wide-
I am told that it is 12 feet wide.

Then, I will double it On the basis on which I have started-a sidewalk 6 feet wide, you would have a total of 1,080 square feet. At 16 cents a square foot, that would amount to $172.80. Or double it, and you have 2,160 square feet costing $345.00.
That is what I say-we have paid about double.
And my hon. friend behind me (Mr. Henderson) says that in his town they get this work done for 12 cents. I paid 16 cents for a sidewalk in front of my own house last year.
Did the minister say there were 240 square yards in the lot?
Yes. The other expenditures are wiring and fixtures, $660; furniture and letter boxes, &c., $1,343.09; total expenditure up to October 31, 1907, $21,323.
Were tenders asked for the boxes?
Yes.
I would like to get at the size of this lot.
I told the hon. gentleman I could not give the frontage and depth but the area is 240 square yards.
That is an exceedingly small lot. To pay $200 for a sidewalk on two sides of such a lot would be an enormous price.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) is astray in his arithmetic.

If the lot were 12 yards one way by 20 yards the other way, that would make an area of 240 yards. Reduced to feet, such a lot would be 36 feet front by 60 feet deep. Or, for two sides of the lot 96 running feet. If you make a sidewalk 12 feet wide you would have 1,152 square feet which at 16 cents would be $184.32. I think that arithmetic is pretty nearly according to Sangster.

How much was paid for the sidewalk?
Mr. FOWLER, $750. When I said the hon. gentleman paid about double, I was figuring on the size of the lot he first gave. But it appears now that, instead of paying double, he has paid over four times.
Is the hob. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) speaking of the cost of granolithic pavement from any experience?
Yes, I have built many square feet of it at my own expense around my properties in Sussex.
What does it cost?
Sixteen cents.
What is the depth of the granolithic material?
You measure by surface measure.

But I suppose something would depend upon the location-whether the lot was high and dry or whether you had to go deeper for a foundation.
Mr. FOWLER, Something would depend upon whether you had to build up or not. But the building up is done with gravel which is very cheap material in most places. You do not build up with cement from the bottom. But you would need to build up with gold dust to justify such a price as this.



Mr. TA\ LOR. Our town let a contract at 16 cents to lay granolithic sidewalk on several streets, and some of them had to be raised three or four feet. And my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) says that 12 cents was the ruling price there- 16 cents is an outside price.
Something would depend on the cost of cement and the description of the land.

But why should cement he dearer in Antigonlsh than in other places? In fact, it ought to be less; for. I understand there are cement works in Sydney. There certainly is not enough to account for the difference between 12 cents or 16 cents and the 70 cents that the minister has been paying. It is no wonder that this building, which was to have cost $15,000 or $16,000 has already cost $28,000, if everything else is paid for on the same basis as this sidewalk:
I will have the chief architect produce a plan of the lot and building.
Better let the item stand.

The chief architect tells me that the sidewalk cost a certain sum per foot, and his opinion was that the price was reasonable. I do not profess to know the cost of granolithic sidewalk, because this material is not much used in the part of the province from which I come.
Does the architect say that 70 cents is a reasonable price?
He says that the sidewalk was constructed at a reasonable price, but he did not state at how much per yard. But I will get the plan.
When a building such as this is finished, who receives it for the government and passes the work as having been carried out properly?
The clerk of works would certify to the erection of the building, then the chief architect would send a man from his department to see if it was built according to the plans and specifications.
Who had the contract for the sidewalk ?
I cannot say from this memorandum. But it was let by contract at so much per foot, the total cost being $735. It says, ' Sidewalk, &c.' showing there was something in addition.
Is it the custom of the department to bear the whole cost of the construction of a new sidewalk built in front of a public building ?

The architect tells me that where the work is entirely a new one Mr. FOWLER.
the department has been in the habit of paying the whole cost.
What about repairs to that sidewnlk ? Does the department pay for keeping the sidewalk in repair ?
After the department has constructed the sidewalk the practice is to keep it in repair.

I would call the minister's attention to the sidewalk in Fredericton which extends a whole block on Queen street. The government owns all the property on the eastern side of Queen street from Carleton to Regent street. On this property are the post office building and the officers' barracks, and that sidewalk has been in very bad condition for several years past and is in great need of repairs. It is an asphalt sidewalk.
I shall be glad to give it consideration.
Have you a vault in that building ?

Yes, that is the contract. The vault door is supplied by the contractor.
Mr. FOWLER, You had better let this item stand until we get the particulars.
Very well.
I did not quite understand the answer of the minister as to the procedure after public buildings are finished.

The clerk of works certifies to the department that the building has been completed, and then the chief architect sends an architect from the department to examine the building and see whether it has been completed according to the plans and specifications, and he informs the chief architect of the fact.
Is that satisfactory to the department ?
I think that is the only way in which it can be done.

That explains why so many works turn out to have been badly constructed. They are not finished properly, they are made by people who do not care what happens to them after they are finished, but who construct them according to their own notions. There is no supervision. I remember a case where a public -work was built by men who did not care whether it was well done or not. They have a clerk of works who is generally a political appointment. He is paid $3 a day, and sometimes does not know anything about the work he is supposed to supervise. He makes a report that the building is finished properly, and it is accepted. When I was in the west last summer I heard of a breakwater built by the government at

Nanaimo, at a cost of $10,000. As soon as it was built a freshet came and carried it away, and it is now lying somewhere in the sea.	-
Does the hon. gentleman say a breakwater was built at Nanaimo ?
At a place called Nanaimo, anyway it was in the district of Nanaimo.
Nanaimo is in my constituency, and there is no wharf built by the government there.

It was in the district of Nanaimo. A day or two ago I heard of a lighthouse built by the Department of Marine and Fisheries that has been carried away, a very expensive work. I mention these things to show that the government should pay more attention to these works and see that they are properly inspected before they are accepted.

That is exactly what we are doing. Before a building is accepted the chief architect sends an expert, an experienced man from the department, who makes a thorough examination, and he does not accept the building unless it is built according to the plans and specifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's criticisms may be correct with respect to some other cases of which I have no know-lege, but they are not correct with respect to this building in Antigonisb. He says that these works are often built by people who have no concern but to get them up and get away. This building was erected by Rhodes & Curry, one of the most reputable firms in the lower provinces, and I am sure these gentlemen have sufficient pride in their work not to build it as the hon. gentleman says. There may be some cases that justify his criticism, but as to any work constructed by Rhodes & Curry, who are contractors of the highest standing, there is no ground for criticism.

I was speaking in a general way, and criticising the government for receiving these public works without paying sufficient attention to the way they have been built. It may be that in this case the clerk of the works is a good man. But we all know from what takes place in the Public Accounts Committee that in many cases these clerks of works do not even go near the work.

What has taken place in respect of this building is an index of what takes place in respect of all buildings, as I am informed by the chief architect. In the first place there is a clerk of works appointed. Inquiry is made as to his ability, his judgment and integrity before he is appointed.

And his politics.

Of course we would not like to appoint a man who would endeavour to have a building badly constructed in order to discredit the government. We try to get a man who will be fair at all events, and see that the work is constructed so as to reflect credit upon the government. Then the department sends an expert from time to time to see that everything is being done properly. When the building is finished the clerk of the works makes his certificate, but the chief architect does not act finally upon that, because he sends an expert from the department specially to examine the building carefully, to look it all over, and see if it has been constructed according to the plans and specifications. I do not say that is the only case. The chief architect cannot now say how much was paid, without referring to the notes.
As great a sum as $10,000 ?
