Altogether about $100,000 in 1907-08 for nine months was paid out by the Department of Public Works for outside architectural fees. You had better hire 20 good men at $5,000 each.

I hope the hon. gentleman does not think that by quoting these figures he shows that the chief architect was in error in regard to the amount paid for services of architects last year for purely architectural services. In the items he has read he includes engineering work. Vautelet is an engineer and his work in connection with the St. Andrews lock and at Quebec was engineering work.
At Quebec he was putting up a building.

But that is not under Mr. Ewart at all. .The hon. gentleman has included the amounts paid for prizes for the plans for the large departmental building which it is proposed to construct on Sussex street. I had not in mind the inclusion of these amounts as that is not architects' work in the ordinary sense.
Would not the man who got first prize be the man whose plans were adopted ?
No, it does not follow at all.
Then did you get nothing except plans that you would not use, in return for the money paid out ?

A board of judges was appointed to ask for and consider the plans and to determine as to which were entitled to the prizes, but the department expressly reserved the right to exercise its own judgment as to adopting any of the plans. The department is not bound to take any one.
Did you start a competition among architects for plans for a departmental building and offer prizes to a considerable amount and not propose necessarily to take any of the plans ?
Certainly.

You offered premiums for the making of plans suitable for a departmental building and gave the prizes although the department did not consider one of the plans suitable for erection purposes? That seems to me a funny proceeding. I would think that you would try to get plans as nearly perfect as possible and if an architect could not draw a plan suitable for that building he certainly did not deserve a prize. It is the most surprising statement I ever heard.
Deducting $15,000 for St. Andrews and $12,000 for the plans that still leaves $75,000 for outside architects. I am not blaming the minister, it is simply that he does not get proper information.
The payment to Darling and Pearson was for services extending over some years, not for last year.
The question was what was paid last year ?

The question was put generally one afternoon when we were discussing estimates and the chief engineer said he did not think it would exceed $10,000 a year, taking the average. A number of the other gentlemen who were mentioned by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) supervised the erection of buildings, acting as clerks of works as well as inspectors. As to the plans for the departmental buildings, these buildings will be very costly and*it is desirable that they should he built upon the very best design possible. No one would regard it as unreasonable that prizes should be offered to architects for the submission of plans. Even although the plans received may be departed from in many respects, yet they afford most valuable information to the chief architect and I presume he may take ideas from all of

them. What I meant to say was that the department did not bind itself absolutely to adopt any one of these plans ; it reserved a certain freedom which I think it was desirable to reserve.
Do you have the right to use the plans ?
Oh, yes, I can use any part of them, we can take any part of them we choose.
Were the prizes paid?
Yes, we paid prizes of .$8,000, $4,000, $2,000 and $1,000 ; that is $15,000 in all.

The answer of the minister seems to be very reasonable when he says that the chief architect will have to go through all these different plans. When the Langevin block was built-and it is looked upon as one of the finest buildings in Ottawa, the chief architect at that time, who, I am sure, was not the superior of the present architect, made the plans without consulting anybody. It did not cost the government one cent for making the plans of that beautiful building. To show the difference between the course pursued by the two governments, I might refer to the estimaters who were appointed to value the properties on Sussex street which have been purchased by the government for the site of this new building. I think there were three or four sets of estimaters.
Is the Langevin block the building in connection with which the roof was omitted from the contract ?
Oh, no.

I do not know, I am talking about the plans of the buildings. Three or four sets of estimaters were appointed to value the property on Sussex street. One set of men made an estimate and they were paid and very well paid. Another set of men made a second estimate and they were paid, and then Mr. Riopel was appointed to make a new estimate. He was paid a part of his account for services and now he is claiming a very large sum of money. My hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) need not be surprised if money is spent in this way. It all goes to party friends right and left. It is part of the combination.
Notwithstanding the explanation of the minister, which my hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) sarcastically has said was a reasonable answer, and I am sure my hon. friend was sarcastic-
I think the hon. gentleman's statement was sincere.
Certainly.
I had supposed that my hon. friend was speaking sarcastically.
No, I referred to the hon. minister's answer.
Surely my hon. friend is not sincere in saying that the payment of $15,000 to assist the chief architect in drawing up these plans is reasonable ?
I thought that that was a good answer compared with the other things they were doing a little lower down.

I knew my hon. friend was sarcastic. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is so accustomed to giving soft-soapy answers that he always assumes that every thing is all right. Is it not absurd on the face of it ? We pay a chief architect a salary for doing what ?-surely for designing these public buildings that are to be erected. Surely the chief architect has assistants-how many ?-by the score ?
A great many.
How many ?
Twelve who may be called architects and draughtsmen.
The Dominion was not so big then as it is now.

The building is the same whether the country was as big or not.
Mr; PUGSLEY. I mean that the work of the architect's office was not nearly so great then as it is now.
The men were bigger than they are now.
They were very good men.
I cannot conceive of a greater waste of public money than the payment of $15,000 to these outside architects.
Was the competition open to the wrorld or only to Canadians ?
Only to Canadians.
Would my hon. friend give the names of those who made plans and those who got the prizes ?
I could, not give all the names. Twenty-nine different architects submitted plans.
Was there a committee appointed to examine the plans ?
Yes, a committee consisting of the president of the Ontario Association of Architects, the president of the Quebec Association of Architects, and Mr. Ewart, the chief architect of the department.
These were the committee ?
Yes, they were the boai-d of judges.
Were they paid ?
They were paid.
Did they compete ?
No.
How much did they get ? 1 do not think there is any limit to what may be done by this government in the line of wrong-doing.
I knew my hon. friend would say that.

I want to compliment the Minister of Public Works by saying that of all the ministers he is prepared to go to the greatest length in the waste of public money, and I will guarantee, from what I know of the hon. gentleman and his former career, that he will outstrip them all. He will leave them a long way in the distance.
I want to know how much this committee was paid.
This committee was paid $4,500.
Besides the $15,000 ?
Mr. PUGSLEY\ Yes, they were paid $1,500 each.
So that the whole cost about $20,000?
How much money do you propose to expend on this building ?
We will be in that.

I am surprised at the hon. member for Kings and Albert indulging in talk such as he has in regard to the plans. I am sure that my hon. friend, in his moments of sincerity and soberness, and he is always sober and not always insincere, will realize that when the government were undertaking the erection of these very important and costly buildings to accommodate the various departments, and including a palace of justice, it was not an unreasonable expenditure of money to invite from the architects of Canada designs for those buildings. I think also that any one would say that in not binding ourselves to accept any one of those plans, but giving the chief architect of the department the right to avail himself of any ideas which were unfolded by them, the department wras acting wisely. With regard to myself, I am always thankful for any attention that my hon. friend gives me. Even though my hon. friend has at times in the past criticised me and gentlemen with whom I have been associated, I have seen the day when he was the warmest in our praise. Therefore I do not take the criticisms of the hon. gentleman upon myself too seriously. But I think it might be advisable for him to wait until he sees how I administer the department over which I preside before he gives the assurance to this House that I shall not manage it economically and well. Thus far my hon. friend cannot point to anything in my administration of the department which invites his criticism, or even the criticism of those who would look at the matter from a non-partisan standpoint.

Since my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works has read me this lecture, I will devote a few minutes to a reply. In the first place, he makes the challenge that I have been unable to point to any particular thing in which he has shown extravagance as Minister of Public Works. Sir, that was a safe challenge for the hon. minister to throw down. He knows perfectly wrnll that I have had no opportunity yet to know what he has done in his department. He knows perfectly well that until the accounts for the year are produced it will be impossible for us to know just how extravagantly he has conducted the affairs of his department. But I will refer the hon. gentleman to some of

the things which have already occurred, which will bear out the general statement I made to the effect, that whatever extravagance there might be in the various departments of this government, the Department of Public Works, under the superintendence of the present minister, would far outstrip all those other departments in wanton, wilful >waste and extravagance; and, Sir, you will find when the next session comes, and when we have an opportunity to disclose to the public just what the hon. gentleman has done in his department, that the words I have uttered will be verified and more than verified. We had an order in council passed by the government at the request of the hon. gentleman; and we had in this House the other day the humiliating spectacle of the hon. gentleman being compelled to stand up in his place and admit that owing to what had been brought out here by the opposition, his colleagues had taken him by the neck, as it were, and had rescinded that order in council which he had defended upon the floor of parliament. No greater humiliation was ever offered

X do not wish unduly to interrupt my hon. friend, but X can assure him that he is now making a statement which is wholly unwarranted. Whatever was done in passing the order in council, and whatever was done in rescinding it, was done wholly on my initiation and at my recommendation.
I would suggest that we have departed sufficiently from the item before the committee.

I understand, then, that the chairman feels that his minister is getting rather the worst of this, and that although he invited it by making an attack upon me, the Chairman proposes to exercise his right and refuse to allow me the opportunity of answering him. I have much more to say about the hon. Minister of Public Works, and I would like to have an opportunity now of saying it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I have allowed the hon. gentleman to proceed far enough. I realized a little while ago that the discussion was out of order.
You should have stopped your minister, not me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I propose to ask the committee to come back to the immediate item -which is before the committee. I suggest that for the consideration of the committee.
If my hon. friend desires, we will let this item stand, and take up the next.

I would like to finish what I have to say in answer to the hon.
gentleman first. Surely the Chairman does not want me to do the hon. gentleman the discourtesy of not replying to the statement he made.
The hon. gentleman forgets that I was replying to him.

Not at all. The hon. gentleman was making a statement entirely contrary to the fact, and I was pointing out to him his duty under the circumstances. When the government of which he is a member humiliated him by rescinding an order in council passed at his desire, it seems to me that there was only one course open to him as a man of honour, and that was to lay down his portfolio and resign from the government. Surely no other course was open to the hon. gentleman ; but, as some of my hon. friends suggest, he certainly would not do that. The hon. gentleman has waded through too much in order to get this portfolio. He refers to a time when I spoke well of him. There was a time when I perhaps did speak well of the hon. gentleman and of the views which he entertained upon the political questions of the day ; but that time was when he was sailing under a different flag from the one he sails under to-day, not the skull and cross-bones. That was when he was sailing under the Conservative flag and was as strong a Conservative as could be found in this country. As an individual he is a very nice, courteous gentleman ; but the manner in which you speak of the hon. gentleman's politics depends on the period of the hon. gentleman's career to which you are referring. If you are referring to the period from 1873 to 1878, if you happen to be a Liberal, you will commend most strongly his attitude then on the political questions of the day, because there was at that time, no stronger Liberal or supporter of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie from the Atlantic to the Pacific than the hon. gentleman. But, Sir, there came a change in the year 1878; there was a Dominion election on. The hon. gentleman had not at that time changed his political attitude.
Is this modern or ancient history ?

The hon. gentleman is not so old that the history of his political career would necessarily be ancient history.
The hon. gentleman is grey, but he is not really an old man except in sin^-politi-cal sin. I make the distinction. Now, there was a general election on, and any person walking along the streets of the city of St. John and looking at the bill boards might have seen a notice to the effect that there would be a rally of the Liberal party to be held in the hall in the parish of St. Martins, and that rally was to be addressed b'- the Hon. William Pugs-ley and other leaders of the Liberal party. This was the notice that appeared on

Monday. But on Tuesday any person passing through the streets and observing the bill boards would see pasted over this notice a' placard bearing these words : 'Great Conservative Rally ; a meeting in the interests of the Liberal-Conservative party
to be held in the hall of 

 on such a
day ; the chair to be taken at 8 o'clock, and the meeting will be addressed by the Hon. William Pugsley and other Conservative leaders.' Talk about the conversion of St. Paul. It was not a circumstance to that of the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman's was quite as rapid.
But not so thorough.

Not so thorough, as my hon. leader says, because the hon. gentleman was yet to undergo another change, a change equally wonderful, and accompanied by another change of government of course. No government could change more quickly than could the hon. gentleman. Time passed. The hon. gentleman was a strong Conservative; and in 1895-not very ancient history-he had aspirations towards Ottawa. He wanted to be a representative of his native county and he was nominated the Conservative candidate. I had the pleasure of moving his nomination and I had the pleasure on several occasions- and I suppose that is what the hon. gentleman refers to-of accompanying him in his canvass throughout the county and of speaking from different platforms with him. I cannot recall now that I was particularly eulogistic of the hon. gentleman personally, but I certainly was of the policy of the party of which the hon. gentleman then was a strong exponent, as I have always been all my life. So that when he says there was a time when I was somewhat vehement in my praise of his political associates, I admit the fact. But that time was when the hon. gentleman was an associate of mine politically and a leader in that party to which all my life I have belonged.
That does not happen to be what I was referring to.
Then I cannot understand what the hon. gentleman was referring to and would like him to state what it was.
The hon. gentleman knows.

I do not know. But there came a change. The hon. gentleman found that his political course had been so tortuous that the good people of the county of Kings-the Conservative people of the county of Kings-were not satisfied with him as a candidate, and he discovered that if he were to continue a candidate he would be very apt to lose the election. So he wrote a letter to the president of the association in which he resigned the nomination and gave his reasons for resigning.
We had all this four mouths ago.
The hon. gentleman has brought it on himself and he may'have it several times before this parliament is through.
What about the suffering country?

It is a good thing and will bear repetition. The hon. gentleman wrote a letter to the president of the association in which he resigned the nomination and gave his reasons, and his principal reason was that he did not wish to be the means of sowing discord and dissension in the ranks of the grand old Conservative party of which he was such a lover-that party which had done everything that had been done for the upbuilding of Canada. And he went to St. John, and there he ran as a strong opponent of both the government and the opposition. He ran as an independent. Why, he had no confidence, Sir, in you as the leader of the opposition, as the leader of the Liberal party at that time. No man on the government side was one-half so strong in denunciation of you, Sir, and your political ideals as was the hon. minister who is now such a subservient follower of yours.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Stronger than yours ?
Very much stronger. Why there was not a political sin he did not accuse you of. He called you a traitor to your country.

I would not interrupt my hon. friend when he goes to such extremes if he were saying what he really believed to be true, but he is simply indulging in flights of imagination and stating what he must know, if he knows at all what I said, to be without foundation.

I can well understand how this bites, but the hon. gentleman has been forgiven, he has made his peace, he has wiped the feet of the First Slinister with his tears of repentance, he has had the benediction of the First Slinister laid upon his bowed head and has received the injunction :	Rise, son, thy sins are forgiven thee, go and sin no more. This was in the days when the hon. gentleman was in the transition period of his political life. It was in that transition period when he was changing from the caterpillar to the butterfly and when he was still in the chrysalis as a member of the Conservative party. But during that election campaign of 1896 the process of change and disintegration had begun, and when, on the night of June 23, 1896, the news came flashing over the wires that the Liberal party had won, just as quickly as the news came, the hon. gentleman cast aside his caterpillar shell and emerged into the splendor of a

new day, a gaudy, glittering butterfly. He has been a" Liberal ever since. Yes, he has since In the twelve years during which he has been basking in the sunshine that radiates from you, right hon. Sir, as the head of the Liberal party

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Address the Chair.

I am addressing the chair, Sir, through you. Ever since that day he has been a strong, active working Liberal. I want to say, however, to the right hon. the First Minister that I do not think the hon. gentleman has brought very great strength to the Liberal cause in the province from which lie comes. I think, Sir, that the defeat, the disastrous defeat which has befallen the Liberal party in the province of New Brunswick, is to some considerable extent due to the dissatisfaction felt by the people of that province in the political principles and methods of the hon. gentleman whom you have taken into your cabinet as Minister of Public Works. I have no doubt that this had largely to do with it. And that disastrous defeat which has overtaken your party in that province, although it was in the matter of local politics, is yet a true index of what will happen in federal politics this autumn, if you decide to go to the country then. Mr. Chairman, I would advise the Prime Minister to cast about him for a man from the province of New Brunswick in whom the people of that province would have more confidence. I am perfectly disinterested in giving this advice, for, from the party standpoint, there is no one who could probably make it easier for us of the opposition to win in that province than the hon. gentleman. But you had, sitting behind him in the back benches, one man who was able to carry a constituency which he represented here; and it seems to me that if you are looking for political success in the province of New Brunswick, you had better change your Minister of Public Works. For, not only will he be a weakness to you in New Brunswick, but you will find that he will continue in his conduct of his present office the methods which he followed in his own province and which brought his part}' their to disastrous rout. It does seem to me that the condition of your party, owiug to the misconduct of the heads of departments, is already deplorable enough without making it worse by giving a free hand to your Minister of Public Works. This advice I give gratuitously to the Prime Minister ; I give it from the patriotic standpoint, not from the party standpoint.
It is all the more valuable.

It is all the more valuable, for it is all perfectly disinterested. I hope the Prime Minister will profit by it and that he will relegate the hon. gentleman to the
background and bring in a new Minister of Public Works.

I feel that I should really apologize to the House for taking up any time in replying to the observations of the hon. gentlemau (Mr. Fowler) for they are not at all relevant to the matter before the committee. But I wish to say one word in answer to the speech which the hon. gentleman has just made. This is the same speech that was reported in the newspapers some months ago as having been made by the hon. gentleman in St. John before the election was called to fill the vacancy caused by the death of my late friend, Dr. Stockton. On that occasion, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) came to St. John and addressed a large public meeting, maxing the same speech as he has made today. He spoke of my political career, covering some thirty years, and begged the Conservative party to put up some person in opposition to me. But the electors of the city of St. John, Liberals and Conservatives, who know the hon. gentleman and know me, who know7 the course I have pursued in that city siuce I went there to make my home among them a good many years ago, gave the hon. gentleman his answer by returning me by acclamation.

In the first place the statement the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) has made about the speech is absolutely foundationless. I did address a public meeting in St. John, and I did advise the electors to oppose the present Minister of Public Works, even though he had held out as a bribe to the people of St. John w7hat he could do for them if he were returned as Minister of Public Works. And the hon. gentleman plumes himself upon his election by acclamation. I wras opposed to his election by acclamation, notwithstanding all the pledges and promises he made to the people. But, if the hon. gentleman had asked the people to elect him without his portfolio, lie would have been beaten by more than five hundred votes. It w7as not the person of the hon. gentleman that was elected in the city of St. John, it was the office. And is that a thing for the hon. gentleman to plume himself upon? Is that a thing for him to boast about? For my part, I should much prefer to be elected on my personality. Why, the hon. gentleman, never once, during his long political career has appeared before the public and asked for their suffrages as a representative of a party in opposition-Oh, yes; I am mistaken. He did, once. On one occasion he appeared, not exactly as an opposition but as an independent candidate. What happened when lie dared thus to face the electors of any constituency in Canada on his own personality as a man? Why he lost his deposit- that is what happened. This is the hon. gentleman who is trying to make the people think that so magnificent is his personality,

so much are the people of St. John in love with him. that they fall over themselves to elect him by acclamation. Yet, as I have said, the only time that the hon. gentleman ever faced the electors In opposition to any government was when he ran in 1896 as an independent, and was so disastrously beaten that he lost his deposit. Yes, and even if he had got a thousand votes more than he did, he would still have lost his deposit. And that is what the people think of the hon. gentleman's personality in the city in which he lives. But, Sir, here was a government in power: here was a city that had made tremendous sacrifices in order to provide terminal transportation facilities: and here, they felt, was an opportunity to get some assistance in the establishment of further facilities which were required at that port; and so they elected the office of Minister of Public Works, and, unfortunately, they had to take with it the personality of the hon. gentleman who had been selected by the Prime Minister to fill that office. It was a handicap that the office was filled by the hon. gentleman-almost anybody else would have had a better chance than he. I do not think he will refer to this matter again.
Carried.
This item stands, does it?
It is carried.
No, it is not carried; and I do not propose that it shall be carried now. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) promised certain information with regard to it.

Well, let it stand then.
Bridgewater, public building. $22,000.

What is this one to cost?
Mr, PUGSLEY. The hon. gentleman will see that this is a revote of $5,000. This is to make provision for the construction of a public building in the town of Bridgewater. The total cost will be $39,500, including the site, heating, electric wiring, fixtures, furniture, &c. This is a new building. Bridgewater is in the county of Lunenburg.
How much did the land cost ?
$5,500. The lot is 110 feet on King street, and 130 feet on Dominion street.
What is the population of Bridgewater ?

By the census of 1901 the population was 2,900, including Bridgewater North and South. The post office receipts for 1907 were $1,362 ; customs receipts, $4,871 ; money orders issued, $42,449 ; money orders paid, $32,000. It has a large bank, a printing office, four gang sawmills, grist mills, and so forth, and does a large trade in lumber.
Mr.. BERGERON. Who was the site bought from ?
From H. and A. Davidson.
Was that a vacant lot ?
I presume so.

It is perhaps fair to say that the price is large ; I suppose judged by the land values in most Nova Scotia towns it would appear to be large. But there were few available places on which this building could be erected, and it appeared desirable to have it built on the principal business street which is somewhat congested owing to physical conditions, and consequently the values on this street are higher than in most Nova Scotia towns. This vacant lot cost the owners practically the amount it was sold for. I had considerable to do in advising the department concerning the purchase of the lot. The owners, in making up the price, took into consideration the original cost, and interest at 4 per cent.
Who did the Davidsons buy the property from ?
A corporation known as the Academy of Music Company, Limited, I think were the previous owners. There was an opera house upon the site at one time and it was burned.
Who selected the site ?
I recommended the site to the department. It appeared on the whole to be the best site in the town, and no other site could be purchased at a lower price.
Did the Davidsons buy the property on purpose to sell it to tile government ?
No, I may say that the Davidsons sold this land at a lower price to the department than they would have sold to any other purchaser.
How long had the opera house been burnt before this property was soli to the government'?
About seven or eight years.
What lawyer put the title through ?
I do not think that is mentioned.
I suppose this building is being erected by tender ?

Yes, tenders were received in answer to public advertisements. The tenders were $23,500 and $24,000, the lowest being accepted. The tenderers were A. D. Falconer, of Sydney, and W. R. Macdonald, of Kentville.
How much was paid for legal services for getting the title ?
The total amount paid for legal expenses and advertising, printing, survey of site, &e., of every kind were $216.81.
Who was the clerk of works, and what was his salary ?
The clerk of works is Mr. Lamb, and his salary is $3.50 a day.
On whose recommendation was he appointed, and what are his special qualifications for that work ?
I may inform the hon. gentleman that I had the pleasure of recommending the appointment. He is a carpenter, and very competent.
This is certainly a departure from the usual rule, actually appointing' as clerk of works a man whose occupation would fit him for that position.
Are we to understand that the policy of the department is to ask the member for the county to recommend a site for public buildings, and also to recommend the clerk of works ?

As I understand the practice of the department, when a man is required to supervise the erection of a public building, the member of thei county is supposed to know the men best qualified for that purpose, and he is consulted.' If he makes a recommendation the head of the department makes inquiry as to the man's capability, his occupation and generally as to his qualifications for performing the duties.
Does it make any difference on which side of the House the sitting member is ?
I would think so, yes, that is a time-honoured custom.

I might remind the minister that I made a recommendation for the enlargement of the St. John post office, which has not been acted upon. I offer the suggestion to the Minister of Public Works to bear it in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would suggest to my hon. friend that he should not press that because we are told these things are bribes to the citizens of St. John and it would be highly improper to bribe them.

The people of St. John could accept an enlarged post office which is very much needed even although the Minister of Finance may possibly consider that it was being used as a bribe. As the west is absorbing some of our immigrants, so we may be able to absorb an enlarged post office without any injury to the political atmosphere of the city.

The improvement of the accommodation of the St. John post office came under consideration some little time ago, and the Postmaster General decided that increased accommodation is to be given and that is to be attended to. By making certain changes in the interior of the building it is supposed the accommodation can be so improved that it will do for a number of years to come, without going to the heavy expense of erecting a new post office.
Is it the policy of the minister to purchase sites and to appoint clerks of works solely on the recommendation of the sitting member ?

I thought I had made it clear that 'the policy of the department, certainly my policy, is to make inquiries after tlie recommendation is made. We would not act on the recommendation of a member without making inquiry as to the suitability of a site. While ordinarily we feel that we may rely on the recommendations of our friends, in this case we would think it well to go further and make inquiry as to the site for the building and as to the qualification of the clerk of works.
What would the minister think of the selection of a medical practitioner to superintend the erection of a lighthouse ?
Everything would depend on his general qualification, but if he had had experience in that kind of work and knew how to handle men he might be a very good man.
Would it make any difference if he were a defeated candidate ? Would that make his qualifications any stronger ?
I suppose not.
In Sunbury a medical man who has been a candidate in the last two elections was appointed to superintend the erection of a lighthouse.
That is not in my department.
Or wharfs?
Wharfs but not lighthouses. If the hon. gentleman says I appointed a medical gentleman to inspect a wharf he is misinformed.

subtopic: RELIEF OF EDITH MAUD ROSARIO GAMMELL.

speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 139), for the relief of Edith Maud Rosario Gam-mell.-Mr. Galliher.

subtopic: RELIEF OF EDITH MAUD ROSARIO GAMMELL.
speechtext:
I suppose that the committee to whom was referred this case have taken into consideration the evidence perhaps more fully than the Senate Committee did. I called attention the other night to the fact that the evidence that was presented to us from the Senate did not appear
to be very satisfactory, and that view was concurred in by some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who are not present to-night. I do not belong to that committee and do not know what their procedure is; but as the matter was before the Senate Committee, there were to my mind two serious defects in the case. One was that there was no proper identification of tile husband. Taking it as clearly established that improper relations were shown to have existed between a certain man and a lady, it was not definitely shown that the man referred to was the husband of this Mrs. Gammell, although she speaks of him as her husband. Aside from that, the evidence produced was to my mind of the most unsatisfactory kind. It was the evidence of a constable and some one who accompanied him. and it was not explained how they were able to proceed to the point they spoke of without being detected by the other party. I would not believe their evidence for the purpose of determining the ownership of a barrel of apples. It is possible that the members of the House of Commons Committee have satisfied themselves by further investigation; but if they have not, 1 venture to say that this thing is going through on very unsatisfactory and inconclusive evidence.

subtopic: RELIEF OF EDITH MAUD ROSARIO GAMMELL.
speechtext: This Bill is in my name. I may say that I do not know very much about the facts and nothing about the people. I happened to be on the Private Bills Committee when It went through there, and I have also read the evidence. There is something in what my hon. friend opposite says. Still, after all, I think the fact is pretty clearly established that the man with whom the lady was found was certainly not her husband, whoever her husband may have been. With regard to how the people got there without being seen, that would probably depend a good deal on the preoccupation of the individuals themselves as they took their evening stroll. For my part, although the evidence is not as direct as possible, It leaves no doubt In my mind that the woman is entitled to the relief she claims. I may say that there was no further evidence adduced before the committee.

subtopic: RELIEF OF EDITH MAUD ROSARIO GAMMELL.
speechtext:
I submit to my hon. friend's superior judgment in the matter.
