House in Committee of Supply.
Halifax immigration building-renewals and repairs in connection with heating, plumbinw &c„ $1,800.
['We will proceed with Supply and take up the estimates of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works.']

This is for certain repairs to the heating apparatus. The total cost is $4,800 and there has been expended, under a previous vote, $3,000. We are asking for a revote of $1,800 to complete.
Halifax immigrant detention building, $7,-
Is there a larger garrison at Halifax now than when the imperial authorities had charge ?

1 would have to refer my hon. friend to the Minister of Militia for that information.
000.

This is required to complete the building under construction. It is for the treatment of immigrants suffering from trachoma and other kindred diseases. It was put under contract October, 1905. The dimensions are 115 by 51. Total probable cost, $72,106.91. It has been all paid for with the exception of this $7,000.
It is difficult to understand why this expenditure should be necessary now when the accommodation was sufficient for the imperial troops ?
This is not for a new building but for a reconstruction of the old one.
Were the barracks burnt down ?
I thought that we deported the diseased immigrants.
No, but they had become very dilapidated.

They have to be detained until they can be deported and there must be a place in which to treat them. They have to be treated in a humane manner. In some cases they might be detained until they recover.
Halifax military buildings, Wellington barracks-re-construction of married men's quarters, $45,000.
This amount was voted last session but no part of it has been used so that this is a revote. This work is urgently requested by the Department of Militia.
Will tenders be called ?
Yes.

There cannot be very much urgency when the whole amount voted last year remains unexpended. Why was this work held over ? Is there any special object in keeping it on hand until this year ? This money should have been spent when parliament ordered it. We are not supposed to vote money for the mere pleasure of voting it. Why has the minister allowed this work to stand over ? If it was so urgently required, why was it not done last year ? Is the money to be spent this year ?

We intend spending the money this year. It does not always follow that when parliament votes money for a specific purpose, it is absolutely essential that the money should be spent. In view of the financial conditions the world over last year, one can well understand that we should incur only such expenditure as was absolutely necessary.
Suppose there should be no elections this year, will the money be spent just the same ?

The question of an election has never been thought of in this connection.
Halifax-new public building, customhouse, $12,000.

As hon. gentlemen will see, this is a revote of $12,000, to make provision for the amount estimated to be spent during the fiscal year in the erection of a public building in Halifax for the purposes of the customs. I need not go into a description, but may say generally, that it is a large and fine building.
What is the total cost?
Including electric wiring, heating, elevator, furniture, &c., the cost will be $325,015.25.
Who is the contractor?
Mr. Keefe, of Halifax.
Has the contractor done his work satisfactorily to the architect?
Not entirely so. Some objections have been raised. At my request the chief architect has sent a member of his staff to make a thorough investigation, and, in the meantime, an amount is held back.
What is the trouble ?

I suppose the hon. gentleman would not wish me to go into the details. A number of objections are made, none of great magnitude. For instance, there is an objection to the way the windows are hung and a number of matters of that kind.
What was the estimated cost of this building?
My deputy informs me that it was $300,000.
And this has already been exceeded by $25,000.
Well, the estimate of $300,000 was for the bare building, whereas the figure I have given of the building complete includes electric wiring, fittings, furniture, elevator, heating, and so on.

I would draw the minister's attention to a point that has frequently been discussed in this House in past years in connection with the construction of buildings of this kind. I, for one, and others also, have insisted, when a vote is to be taken for a public building, that the minister in charge shall give an estimate of the total cost, not merely for the construction of the building, hut covering also the heating apparatus and fittings, and so on, so that we may know exactly what we are doing, and keep a proper check upon the expenditure of the minister. From the little information I have, this seems, to be one of the cases where the amount necessary to complete the building will far exceed the original estimates. Already more than $25,000 over the estimate has been spent, and now we are asked for another vote of $12,000. Next year, possibly, we may be called upon for a further vote for furniture, and for extras possibly. I presume the minister was not personally responsible for the expenditure on this work, but, of course, he has to assume responsibility for the acts of his predecessors. I wish to make our position clear in this matter. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is very fond of charging hon. members on this side with objecting to public works, especially public works in the province of Nova Scotia. I want the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) to distinguish between objection and criticism. We do not object to the construction of useful public works, for we recognize that expenditure on this service is necessary and will be necessary in time to come. We approve the construction of public works that are essential for the purposes of the country. But we are ready to enter our very strong protest against any extravagance or waste, or, if the minister will pardon me, graft, in connection with the construction of these buildings. This is the reason why we want to have a careful estimate made before any money is voted for the construction of a new building. We find it necessary, owing to the largely increasing expenditure, to put checks upon it. What we object to is not expenditure that is called for by the needs of the country, but careless and extravagant expenditure. As the items of supply are discussed from time to time, the hon. minister will understand why it is that we hold him strictly to account for any over-stepping of the estimate of the cost of a public building. There is no reason why an architect should not estimate almost to a nicety, the cost of a building such as this. A few years ago, we endeavoured to get the Minister of Public Works to erect in small country towns for post office purposes buildings that, probably, would not cost more than SS.000 or $10,000. Hon. Mr. Tarte, when Minister of Public Works, declared his intention of providing such buildings. He made an attempt, commencing, I believe, in West Huron, with the town of Clinton. He proposed to erect there a building on the principle I had suggested, being not only a building for the post office, but a residence for the postmaster, thereby saving the expense of a caretaker. But X understand that when the matter went to the architect he refused to draw the plans and said they were not in the habit of drawing plans and specifications for buildings of less than $10,000. Were I Minister of Public Works-which I do not expect ever to be -I would ask the architect, in such a case, to step out, and would put another man in his place, for I think the minister is the man to be responsible for the expenditure and not the architect. Of course, I find no fault with the officer who is here to advise the minister to-night. Probably that may be the custom. But it is a custom we must try to get over. The architect must be ready to lay before the committee a careful and correct estimate of the total expenditure of the building, and then it will be the duty of this committee, year after year, as we are voting money, to see to it that the expenditure is kept within that line. If tnis is done, I think the Minister of Finance will not encounter the difficulty in furnishing the money for these public works which he has indicated. I was a little surprised when the minister made this confession a few moments ago that the reason why an item of $45,000 was not expended was that the Minister of Finance realized that, owing to- danger of money stringency, it was better to allow the work to remain unfinished than to undertake the expenditure. I had an idea that this country was big enough and rich enough to carry through any proposition approved by parliament, and I think so yet. When matters of this character come up again, especially on a first vote, the minister will hear from me on the subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman, while well intentioned, is too exacting when he insists that there should be at the beginning a very full estimate as to the cost of the work. There should be a general estimate undoubtedly at the time these estimates are prepared. Even in the case of the public work now under notice, detailed plans could not be prepared ; it would not be the part of wisdom to prepare detailed plans before the appropriation was made. Therefore, the first estimate must necessarily be a preliminary estimate. It need not necessarily on that ground be far from the facts, for it should take into account of course lighting, heating and other items of expenditure. But where you prepare detailed plans later, it is possible that you will find the original estimate is somewhat exceeded, and if the amounts are not too large. I do not think would be any ground for criticism. With regard to the more general question of expenditures, it may happen that

after we have' appropriated the money there are seasons when things are running smoothly and when the Minister of Finance would have no reason to forbid the various spending departments to use the moneys which have been appropriated for the public service. But if it should appear that the expenditure was running high and the revenue was running lower than usual, it would be the part of wisdom in the Minister of Finance to say to his colleagues : Well, although this appropriation is supposed to be at your disposal to deal with in any way you like, you had better hold part of it up until the following year. I think that would be a wise course to pursue under such circumstances.

In this case no part of the appropriation has been expended, no effort was made to go on with the work. With reference to what the Finance Minister has said about the impossibility of estimating exactly what a building will cost, my plan would be that the minister should say to the architect :	We propose
to erect a public building in the city of Halifax, or wherever it is to be erected, for a specific purpose ; it may be a custom house, it may be an armoury, it may be a post office. We propose to spend on that building the sum of $100,000, and that sum must complete the building in its entirety. It must furnish the site, it must put up the building, it must furnish the heating, lighting, fittings and everything else required. He says to his architect: I want you to draw a plan and prepare specifications for a building that will cost $100,000 and not one dollar more. If the architect finds, after working out his details, that the building is going to cost a little more than that, then it will be his duty to shave it down, to revise his calculations, and come within the limit of the amount the minister has directed him to expend on that building. I remember years ago when Hon. Mr. Sutherland was Minister of Public Works drawing his attention to this matter in a case that occurred in the city of London, where an estimate for an armoury had been exceeded, if I remember rightly, some $75,000 or $80,000 over the appropriation voted by parliament. I laid down this very principle, and Mr. Sutherland heartily endorsed it. I have no doubt that the Minister of Public Works to-day, if he thinks the matter over, will see a great deal of wisdom in it, and I think he w ill find less trouble in the erection of these buildings and keeping them within the estimated cost if he adopts some arbitrary plan like that. At the same time, I think he will get over the difficulty that the Minister of Finance has pointed out, about a building costing a little more than was originally intended. Let the architect make some allowance for such extras as might reasonably be expected, and hold him re-Mr. FIELDING
sponsible for keeping within the amount that is to be expended on that building.

1 cannot help expressing my extreme surpx-ise at the remarkable statement made by the Minister of Finance. We are now told plainly that when this government comes down with a proposition to parliament to build certain works, no matter what we are told as to the estimated cost, we are not to rely upon that, it doesn't amount to a row of pins. You do not expect your officers to know what to think or to estimate. Just give parliament something to go upon and we will start out. I say that such preaching from the Finance Minister can have no other result than the waste, plunder and extravagance that we have seen for years under this government. The officers of the Department of Public Works are present and are listening to the Finance Minister. The architect hears the Finance Minister of this country standing up and giving him practically authority just to shuflle off the figures. No matter whether we are right or wrong, just give us something to throw out to the House and we will go on with the work. Now, that is so extravagant a proposition that I wonder the Minister of Finance is not ashamed to stand up and make it. Why, such a proposition would disgrace any municipal council. The idea of a municipality going to work to build a municipal structure, and without ascertaining what that structure was going to cost, committing the municipality to the work, going on and putting $10,000, $20,000 or $30,000 upon it. Now, you have begun it you must go on with it, though it cost you $100,000. I hope the hon. gentleman spoke without any consideration and simply to get the Minister of Public Works out of a possible hole he was in, because I think the hon. gentleman knows a great deal more about business than one would imagine from that statement. Surely there cannot be anything plainer than that before a minister controlling a department would recommend his colleagues to construct a particular public work, he would take the utmost care with his officers to find out what it would cost before he dared to come before his colleagues in council to get their approval. He should be able to tell them what it would cost; he might not be able to guarantee the expenditure to a dollar. But what do public companies, what do municipalities, what do governments do who have any care for their reputation ? They get from their engineer a carefully prepared estimate of the cost of the construction in detail ; they add a percentage to that to cover all possible contingencies, say ten or fifteen per cent. The engineer or architect who would lead his company into exnenditures that would ultimately upset all their calculations would get his walking ticket very quickly. But

this government could not dismiss an architect no matter how far he might be out, because the Finance Minister says :	Oh,
we do not expect him to be correct; we simply get something to go upon, to start with. They would rather he did not estimate too closely because as it is they can come session after session and say :	We
only got $50,000 from you and now we want $100,000 more. I think it is an outrage upon the House that we should be asked to vote money on an estimate which according to the words of the minister of the department goes for nothing.
Who said that ?

Because the Finance Minister says that we must not pay attention to that estimate, we cannot be accurate so we need not pay attention to the estimate, but simply vote what is asked for. Over and over again we have been asked to vote fifty per cent, sixty per cent or 100 per cent more than we have been told the work would require, only to be told afterwards that it was simply a rough estimate to start with, and that it could not be expected that the officers would know from the beginning the probable cost. That is just what the architect is for. Here is an architect who is building a post office. He has probably had 20 samples of that very building all through the country and should not have the slightest excuse for not coming very close to the proper figures in his estimate ; but if he is told, as the Minister of Finance says, to go ahead, he will not take the trouble to be accurate, he will simply put in any sum, it would be quite superfluous for him to make an accurate estimate as he can have all he wants added to his original estimate. The Minister of Public Works says that thei'e was an estimate for this building, but they did not put in the wiring. He might just as well say that they did not put in tile gas pipes, or the cement that was provided long before the completion of the building. The wiring forsooth. I venture to say that we will probably have this up next year with a request for several thousands more to put in the patent steel desks. The argument of the Minister of Finance will be quite as effectual next year or five years hence, we will have something in addition to the original estimates under the name of furniture. This year it is wiring ; I suppose the next time it will be door knobs, window panes or something of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What the Minister of Finance thinks will be judged from what he said and what is in ' Hansard ' and not from the extraordinary distortion of his words we have heard from the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker).
I am pretty accurate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. 'member is not accurate, and if any one takes the 227
trouble to consult ' Hansard ' and to read the extraordinary statement the hon. gentleman has made, he will see that the hon. gentleman was not accurate. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) to whom l was replying, said that the Minister of Public Works in asking a vote for a public building such as the one now asked for at Halifax, should lay before the House full and detailed plans and estimates of the building, and condemned the minister for not producing such plans. I stated that my hon. friend had a purpose in that which was legitimate and commendable, but it was not well to push that contention too far. I said it was not the practice and it had never been the practice of any government, when a first vote is taken for a public building, to come forward with all the detailed plans. It would not be the part of wisdom to undertake the detailed plans of a public building before parliament had made an appropriation.
Why not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has never been done, i do not think it is possible.
It should be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree. If we could all be as wise as the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) it would perhaps be better but that is impossible.
How is he to get tenders for the building if he has not plans ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At the time you are asking for an appropriation you are not asking for tenders. I am not speaking of the time when you ask for tenders, but of the time when you take the first vote in parliament, months before tenders are asked for. Of course when tenders are asked "you must have detailed plans down to the duest point. But when application is made to parliament for the construction of a building of a certain character in a cerium place. I do not think it is reasonable to ask a department to have detailed plans for presentation. It has never been done and I do not think that any sensible man would ask it. When you come to call for tenders that is the proper time to have detailed plans and specifications made. If it turns out that the original preliminary and general estimate, which should include wiring and all these things, turns out to be less than is required, it does not prove that the architect is incompetent or that the minuter neglected his work.
Mr. *BLAIN. I see at Y-36 an item :
Department of Customs, duty on bronze coat-of-arms, $435.
Would the minister explain that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I remember that a coat-of-arms was included in the plans for the building, and the contractor suggested that



lie should be allowed to bring it in free of duty. I know my own view was that as he had tendered to put in a eoat-of-arms, therefore lie should pay duty. I thought the Department of Customs should make him pay that and I think they did.
The item, as it is worded, shows that the duty was paid.
By whom ?
By the contractor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be paid I take it for granted, to the contractor, as a part of the general cost, but he would have to pay the duty to the customs.
Would that be charged against him ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It should be and I suppose it was.
It would probably be paid by the Department of Public Works and charged to the contractor.
I cannot understand why it should be in this book any more than 10() kegs of nails supplied to the contractor.

My deputy tells me that the duty was paid by the department. The department at the time insisted that the contractor should pay it. There was a long argument and finally it was decided that under the circumstances the department should bear the duty. It was not paid by the contractor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that statement is correct I must withdraw what I said. I know the contractor mentioned the matter to me and I told him that he would have to pay the duty. I never heard of the matter since. I supposed that he had paid it.

The contractor tenders for the coat of arms upon the building and he decides to purchase this coat of arms in New York. May I ask the minister how ' much the coat of arms cost or how much the contractor's tender was ?
My deputy says that the ground upon which the contractor made the claim that he should not pay the duty was that formerly goods for the government came in free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was so formerly.
The contractor urged that he did not suppose there would he any duty upon the coat of arms.
How much did it cost when the duty was $435 ?	,
The hon. gentleman would know pretty nearly as well as I would.
About $1,500.

Probably, or perhaps more than that.
Mr. FIELDING
At what rate of duty would this be admitted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be 20 to 25 per cent.
At all events he did not suppose the government would exact the duty. That is the argument he made and the minister at that time yielded to the argument and allowed the duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that I misled the committee, because I supposed that he would he required to pay the duty. That was the impression I had and I did not know that he had persuaded the department to adopt his view until the statement was made by my hon. friend.
Why did he not purchase this coat of arms in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are these goods made in Canada?
I think they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not.
With all due respect to the hon. the Minister of Finance I am sure they are.
Will the hon. gentleman say where they are made in Canada?
In Toronto. I had something to do with the purchasing of one myself although not so extensive as this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would it be suitable for a large building?
For the court house in my own town.
St. John, New Brunswick, is another place wThere they make them.
The chief architect tells me that it could not be got in Canada at that time.
If it could not be got in Canada the architect should have changed the plan so that it should he manufactured in Canada.
I am quite sure that it would have been obtained in Canada if it had been possible because the artist who made the model was a Canadian. He obtained it from the United States.

I notice that a clock was purchased at a cost of $2,080. It was also brought in from the United States for this building. May I ask the minister if the duty was paid on this clock by the government or the contractor?
The chief architect tells me that the duty on the clock was paid by the contractor and he also tells me that there was no clock of that description manufactured af that time in Canada.
What about the British preference ?
Who was the contractor of the building ?
Mr. M. E. Keefe.
How much has he received 1

The contractor has received $251,928. While I am upon my feet I may say that I am sure that if my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) had wished to make any argument in regard to the chief architect's estimates being exceeded he certainly was very unfortunate in taking the case of this particular building, because it happened in this case that the chief architect made his estimate before calling for tenders and after he had prepared his plans and his estimate was $300,000 exclusive of the site. As a matter of fact the building will be completed with the additional $12,000 which we are asking for and the total cost of the building will only be $325,000, which includes site, inspection and everything, showing that the chief architect was only $1,000 out of the way.

That is not an answer at all to the remarks made by my hon. friend from Hamilton and which were replied to with so much heat by the hon. the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding). I do not know why the hon. the Minister of Finance found it necessary to work himself into such a passion, such a rage. Whether it was actual rage that he felt or only simulated passion that he exhibited I do not know. Certainly my hon. friend from Hamilton did not distort the early statement that was made by the hon. the Finance Minister. It was a very unfortunate statement in view of the fact that the chief architect was here listening to him because it seemed as if it were a warrant to him to pursue the ordinary slipshod methods which have been hitherto pursued with respect to estimates for public buildings. Why there should be a different mode of procedure adopted for the conduct of a work by the government from that which would be adopted by a corporation or municipality with respect to the construction of public works is something I fail to understand; and I do not think the Minister of Finance, in his violent philippic, made it at all clear why there should be this difference. Why should it not be possible for the chief architect, who has a large staff regularly employed in his department, besides the outside staff that he employs, including several persons of his own name-I do not know whether they are his own relatives or not, before coming to this House to ask for an appropriation, to make a closer estimate of the actual cost ? Instead of that we find in every one of these public works that the cost is far in excess of the original estimate. I re-227*
member a somewhat famous case of a public work in the province of Quebec, a work known as the wharf at Grande Vall&e ; the first estimate we had was (lie exceedingly moderate sum of $5,000, and yet we paid out about $75,000 before we got through with that work. Now, I understood that this $75,000 of work at Grande Vallee has been carried away and is not in existence. However, the purpose for which that wharf was built having been served, I suppose the government did not care what became of the wharf.
Who told the hon. gen. tleman that yarn that it has all been carried away ?
I have the statement of my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor).
Does he say that the Grande Vallee wharf has been carried away ?
Part of it fell into the river and a great deal of expenditure was necessary to replace it.
The hon. member for Kings and Albert said just now that it had been carried away.

The Minister of Public Works does not think anything about a portion of this work falling into the river because they are so accustomed to their works dropping into the river that it does not excite comment.
The object was attained ; the limits were sold.

It was necessary to carry a certain county in Quebec and there was only one man who could carry it for the Liberal party. So, an arrangement was made whereby this gentleman was to have a wharf built at Grande Vallee in order that he might dispose of certain limits which he had purchased and which though valueless without this wharf, might be given value and might be disposed of. The bargain was carried out ; the county was carried ; the wharf was built. Now it does not make any difference whether it drops into the river or not, because the limits were sold after the wharf was built.
Is my hon. friend aware that the Deseronto people are carrying on large lumbering operations there ?

I do not know ; I think not. But it does seem to me that the minister has not done himself proud by the stand he has taken on this question. He has had to change his position in regard to this coat of arms, and he will find It necessary to change his position with respect to the duty on the clock, because I take it that was paid by the government.
I do not know.
At any rate, the duty m the coat of arms was paid by the government, and the Minister of Finance said he thought improperly so.

At page V-36 of the Auditor General's Report there is this item:
' Schulze, C. G. & Co., Est. 1 to February 16, on $2,080 contract for clock and $268.80 duly.'
Mr. P1JGSLEY. That does not show that the government paid the duty.

If would look as if the duty was paid by the government and was charged against the contractor ; but as far as the coat of arms is concerned, the duty was paid, and the Minister of Finance says it should not have been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Generally speaking, I think the admission of various articles for the government free of duty has been a source of much embarrassment, and in the tariff as it now stands we have insisted that everything shall pay duty, even w'hen a department imports the goods. I recollect the contractor saying that he thought this coat of arms ought to be free of duty. I said that I thought it should pay the duty. He evidently went to the department and was able to satisfy the department on the general principle that goods for the government ought to be admitted free of duty.

The other people who tendered would naturally expect to pay duty, and therefore this contractor was given that advantage over them. It does seem a funny thing that you had to go to the United States to get the coat of arms of the country cast in bronze. Surely there are brass founders in this country who can cast a coat of arms.

I have some information about the manner in which this work was done, and I want to read a paragraph :
The floors of the building-
Will the hon. gentleman tell me from what he is reading ?
From private information which I have, that is good information, I may say.
Will the hon. gentleman kindly let me know from whom the information proceeds ? It would be valuable to me. I am very desirous of getting information of that kind.

I am equally anxious to communicate the information to the minister. The only question in which my hon. friend and I are interested is whether these statements are correct or not. The hon. gentleman has already opened the door by saying that the department is not satisfied with the work done by Mr. Keefe. Was the contractor paid any extras on this work ?
He has not been paid any extras on this work.
Will he be paid any ?
He has a claim against the department which has not been recognized so far.
Is it decided that his claim will not be paid ?

I have asked the chief architect to send one of his staff to Halifax to examine the building, and into the complaints that have been made. The matter of the balance of the contract is under consideration, and his claim is also under consideration.
It is not settled one way or the other ?
No.
What is the amount of the claim for extras ?
I do not remember at this moment.
The item on page Y-36 of the Auditor General's Report says that $268.80 of duty was paid, and $1,560.80 was paid on account.
It seems from this account very clear that the contractor paid the duty, and he received an estimate on both. The duty is added to the cost of the clock.
Why would the duty be mentioned there at all ?
It is there because it shows the payment made to the contractor, who is paid on progress estimates. The duty is added to the contract price.
If you add the duty to the contract price, would not that be making the government pay it ?

Not at all. What apparently took place was this. The contract price was $2,080. Adding the duty, $268.80, would make about $2,340, and upon that the Public Works Department made a payment of $1,560, leaving a balance due the contractor of about $800.

Why should the duty ippear in the public accounts at all if it
was not paid by the department ?

Does not my hon. friend understand that if the contractor agreed to furnish the clock for $2,300 including the duty, the department would pay him the amount required for the duty ? No doubt, in making this contract, he would take the duty into consideration and regulate his price accordingly.

Why should the word ' duty ' be there at all if the duty was paid by the contractor ? Surely you have some

information as to what the price of the clock was. What was the contract price ?

I have said that the furnishing of the clock was not included in the contract for the building but there was a separate contract. The Schultze Company agreed to furnish the clock at a certain price with the duty added, and the amount of the duty would be added to the contract price of the clock.
Is the government not paying for it ?
Yes, it is paying the duty-in the price of the clock.
In what respect does this differ from the coat of arms?

The coat of arms was in the original contract. That is the difference. Suppose the coat of arms had been ordered separately and Mr. Keefe had said he would take $500 for it and the duty, if the duty were $100, that would have to be added to the contract price. In one sense the government would be paying the duty but the duty would be added to the contract* price. If the government buys the article, it pays the duty because the duty is added to the price. A merchant always adds the duty to the price when selling his goods.
When this contract was made, there would be no question at all about the duty because the contractor would buy the clock in Canada.
No such clocks are made in Canada. It had to be imported and the duty paid on it.
Does the minister say that the contract price was so much and the contractor was to add the duty and would be paid the duty ?
I cannot tell at the moment.
We should have that information. The chief architect does not appear to know much about it. It is rather strange that these clocks could not be made in Canada.
What is the meaning of the words ' less draw-back $8.80 ' ?

I cannot tell my kon. friends what they mean, but I suppose the meaning is this. The amount of the contract was $2,080 and the amount of duty $268.80 or about $2,300 altogether and the amount paid on account was $1,568.80. Then the department always keeps back a certain percentage as an additional security for the completion of the contract, and that $8.80 would be the amount kept back.
If your chief architect cannot invent a better explanation than that, he is not very expert.
This is not the chief architect's statement but my own supposition.
I am sorry you cannot do better than that. Just imagine $8.80 kept back as security for the carrying out of the contract. Well, we will let it go at that.
There is a certain percentage kept back, and the $8.80 may have been required to complete the percentage.
What is the percentage ?
Usually 10 per cent.
10 per cent on what amount ?
This $8.80 may have been required to make up the 10 per cent. Will my hon. friend make a better excuse ?
I would suggest that this was 10 per cent kept back on the price of the pendulum.
Is it a new building entirely ?
Yes.
You have bought a great deal of furniture from Blander, Morris & Company. How many employees are there in that building ?
I do not know, but in a city like Halifax there is a large business done in the customs.
Is this used for the customs ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Chiefly but there are other offices as well.
The exports were $7,000,000 last year and the imports $6,500,000.
Where was the customs done before?
In the building now to be used for a post office.
What has become of the furniture in the old building? This is ail new.
I am sorry to say I cannot tell my hon. friend.
We are buying new furniture all the time and do' not know what becomes of the old furniture.
I presume it would remain in the old post office building.

The minister deserves a good deal of sympathethic treatment. He is new to his position and evidently does not know much about this, and he is not getting any assistance from his officers who are here. I do not know whether it is because these gentlemen are equally ignorant. What the minister had better do is ask

the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, in order that he may obtain some information which he can then give to the House. Here is this matter of the clock. They do not seem to know the contract price or whether the government paid the duty or where the clock was purchased. Then the minister cannot explain what this drawback of $8.80 means. I think the deputy minister might hunt up this information and be in a position to give it to the minister who could then inform the House when we meet again.

Having made the statement that the contractor did not do the work satisfactorily to the department, X want to draw the attention of the minister to this letter which I have received :
The floors of the building sagged shortly after its construction owing to the beams not being set well into the wall. One floor, through which an elevator has to pass, projects over three feet into the space which should be left open to accommodate the elevator. As this projection is thjee feet beyond tbe lower floor, it would require a corkscrew elevator to reach the top floor of the building.
Do any of the complaints which the department has against the contractor refer to any of the items I have read or is it another matter that the department objected to ?

After reading the report of the expert sent to Halifax to examine the building, I should think that the gentleman who wrote that letter had been making himself familiar with the corkscrew, for it is a most exaggerated and unfair statement. The report of the architect does not bear out the statements made.

The minister has said that the contractor did not do his work satisfactorily to the department. As a proof of that, we have the fact that the department held back some of the money. This article goes on to say :
The woodwork in the office desks has come to pieces in parts of the building. The roof was badly constructed, and Keefe charged for extras in the work which should have been included in .the original contract. I think there is no place made for connection with the water mains.
It says also :
The people in the city of Halifax are generally disturbed about the manner in which the contractor has carried on his work.
I would like to know from the minister how much money has been kept back ? Also, does the department intend to allow extras to this contractor who has done his work in such an unsatisfactory manner ?

I have already stated that an expert has been sent from the de-Mr. FOWLER.
partment to Halifax to examine the building. His report has been received, and, while it shows that in quite a number of particulars the contractor has not carried out the specifications, yet the defects are not of the exaggerated kind that the statement given by my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) would lead the committee to believe.
Was there a clerk of works ?
Yes.
Did he report that the work was not right ?

Mr. FOWLER. Mr. PUGSLEY. Mr. FOWLER. Mr. PUGSLEY.
No.
Who was he V Mr. Bush.
What is his business ? He is an architect.
What salary did he receive for this work?

He was to receive 1J per cent on the cost of the building. There is quite an amount held back pending the consideration of the report. We have refused to consider the claim for extras in the meantime.
Is this inspector still employed in the work ?
No.
He is dismissed ? Has he been paid his li per cent on the cost of the building ?
Not in full.
How much is left ?
i could not say at the moment just how much, but it is a substantial amount.
The hon. gentleman will look it up ?
I will write my hon. friend a letter, giving the facts.

I would call the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the following item on page V-36 of the Auditor General's Report:
Robertson, Wm., & Son: steel beams. &e., 1,805 pounds at 7i cents; ladders, $20, $155.38.
How could you put steel beams in a building when the contract has been given for the whole building ?
I will have it looked up.
Who is the contractor ?
Mr. Keefe, of Halifax.
Is that the local member ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He was years ago, but is not now.

I would call attention to an item on the same page, V-36, covering a charge for hot water heating apparatus complete, $4,798 ; another charge for four hot water boilers at $375 ; headers complete two at $128 and valves $180, then additional heating apparatus as per tender, and also alterations in heating apparatus.
I do not pretend to be an architect, but I believe there is no reason for making such changes in heating apparatus as these, or for having additional tenders for heating apparatus for a building of this size. I would like the minister to ask his architect for an explanation.

I am informed that the post office authorities decided to occupy the basement for the purposes of the post office, which necessitated a change in the heating apparatus. The building is a very large one, and, for such a building, the total cost of heating equipment is not at all excessive. The building is four storeys in height and fronts on three streets, with a frontage of 106 feet on one, 86 feet on another and 107 feet on another.
Did the lot belong to the government or was it bought ?

It was bought for $24,-
000.
Mr. BERGERON1. From whom ?
From Mr. Corbett, of Halifax. This is known as the old city market site.

The minister has stated that the inspector did not direct the attention of the department to the fact that the contractor was not doing his work according to the specifications. Who did direct the attention of the department to this point ?

In addition to the gentleman who specially represented the government on this work, we have a resident engineer at Halifax, who, in the discharge of his duty, gave some information with regard to the building which, we thought, necessitated a very complete examination, and so we sent an architect to make that examination.
I see that the sum of $3,900 has been paid for wiring. Is that the wiring alone, or does that include fixtures ?
That includes fixtures.
Has the minister the contract there to show what it required ?
I will get my hon. friend the contract. The contractors in this case were Messrs. J. A. Dunn & Company, of Halifax.

A few moments ago the minister stated that I had made a mistake in selecting the present item as one upon which to apply the plan I suggested with regard to estimating for public buildings. If I was at all in error in selecting this item, the minister himself is responsible, he not having given the full information to which we are entitled. This shows the necessity of having much more explicit information than is given in these discussions. The minister should familiarize himself thoroughly with all these items so as to be able to give the fullest information. I am glad to know that the minister is able to construct this building within the limits of the estimate. But unfortunately the building is not yet completed, and if there are to be a few more clocks and other extras, possibly he may find his estimate exceeded.

I do not find any fault with my hon. friend. I intended^ in this matter, as in respect to all other items, to be as explicit as possible. But the hon. gentleman must remember that I have not been many months in the department. There must be at least a thousand works going on under the control of my department from one end of the country to the other, aDd it is impossible for me to have everything at my fingers' ends.

On page 4, part 3, of the Public Works report, it says : 1 C. E. W. Dodwell, resident engineer and superintendent of public buildings, supervised this work.' Is that the gentleman who called attention to misdoings on the part of the contractor ?
Yes.
The resident architect, Mr. Bush, has he done other work for the department besides this ?
I think this is the first time he has been employed by the department, in recent years at all events.
I do not find any payment to this architect, Mr. Bush. How much has been paid him on account ?
Mr. Bush's services extended over some three or four years, and he has been paid between $3,000 and $4,000 on account.
There is no part of it charged up in this year's Auditor General's report.
He was paid in previous years. I may say that Mr. Bush has been making a claim upon me for the remainder of his commission, and I have deferred payment until the matter was looked into.
How long was the work in course of construction ?

The contract was made on April 16, 1902, to be completed on

September 15, 1904. There was a good deal of delay.
Was there any penalty for failure to complete the contract within the time ?
I think not.
Is it not usual for contracts to contain a penalty clause ?
It is not usual. Security is taken, of course.
What was the cause of the difficulty with Mr. Bush ?

I felt that Mr. Bush was not as attentive to his duties as he ought to be, he did not give as close inspection to the building as I thought he ought to liav. iven. That is the objection I am making to the payment of the balance of his account. He is claiming somewhere in the vicinity of $1,000.
Was Mr. Bush appointed engineer on the recommendation of the local members, as the minister stated this afternoon was the custom of the department ?
I do not know.
Is it not possible to get that information ?
I think not. The minister must take the responsibility of the appointment.
Were there any defects in the building alleged to Mr. Bush as the reason why he should not be paid in full, and what were the defects ?
I cannot tell at this moment.
An hon. gentleman has stated that some defects were pointed out to Mr. Bush, what were the others ?
The hon. gentleman read what purported to be a letter, but I do not know whether the letter was intended as a joke or as an extravagant representation of the actual condition of affairs.

It seems to me this matter ought to be allowed to stand, because the minister has not the necessary information. It seems there has been a great fraud perpetrated upon the public with respect to the building of this custom house in Halifax, and it is a matter of considerable importance.
Mr. PUGSLEV 411 I ask is a revote of $12,000.
The whole thing involved very much more, $300,000. Although the contractor was not erecting the building according to the contract, he has been paid

all except $12,000. The minister must have the certified cheque stiil in his possession and should penalize the contractor. We would like to see all the correspondence between the department and Bush who has so grossly failed in his duty as inspector. If the employment of architects results in this way perhaps it would be as well to continue the old practice of employing tailors and shoemakers as inspectors. It would look almost as if there were collusion between Bush and the contractor. Although you have a resident engineer and a resident architect and presumably sent an architect from the department to inspect for progress estimates, still the work has been so improperly performed that even the department has been forced to take notice of it. I think the item should, stand until we have full information.

I think the hon. gentleman's request is unreasonable. We are asking for a revote of $12,000. Since I became minister the contractor has not received one dollar nor has Mr. Bush. I started investigating immediately the matter was brought to my attention. I sent down a first-class architect from the department who has made a thorough examination. His report does not corroborate the previous reports I have received ; it is to the effect that while there are certain not very serious defects in connection with the roof, the hanging of some of the windows, the flooring in one of the rooms and the cuttings for the elevators, these are so far as I now remember, substantially the only objections he makes. I am taking tile matter up, I am responsible in connection with the chief architect for fully protecting the public and surely nothing would be gained by postponing the passing of this vote. This committee could not give the proper time to the correspondence and therefore it must be left to the minister, and I hope my hon. friend will recognize that it is desirable to get along with public business and to proceed reasonably with the estimates.
Could any one imagine a responsible minister advancing such a reason as that. Even if this committee could not take the time, what Is the Public Accounts Committee for?
It is quite open to the Public Accounts Committee.

Yet we would not have had any information that there was anything wrong if it had not been for a letter received by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain). The minister should at least' have brought the two reports he has received from the architects. It would take a much shorter time to discuss it if the minister had been completely frank with the committee. As I understand, it is notorious in Halifax that the building is be-

ing badly built aud that Bush is iu collusion with the contractor to represent everything as all right when it is all wrong. The opposition have a duty to perform in this House; they should not allow money to be voted unless they are satisfied it is being properly expended.

I think my hon. friend will see that the proper place to take this up is in the Public Accounts Committee. If that committee feel disposed to take it up, I shall see that all the papers are sent there ; but what cause is there to leave this over ?
Mr. POWLEIt. If it comes before the Public Accounts Committee this session I will be satisfied.
You will have to move to get it.
It can easily be got at because there were payments made in 1905-6 and 1906-7 and these are before the Public Accounts Committee.
The department has withheld $12,000. May I ask if that is $12,000 on the original contract ?
I do not think I said $12,000: I said I was not sure of the amount.
Is that part of the money of the original contract ?
Yes.
What proportion of it?
I cannot tell my hon. friend the exact amount to-night.

This is a very large contract and the committee would like to know how much the department has withheld of the original contract. The total amount of the contract is over $300,000. Was there more than one contract ?
There was a contract for fittings also.
Did Mr. Keefe have that as well ?
Yes.
Has Mr. Keefe any other contract with the government in Halifax ?
No.
What is the name of the architect that the department sent down to make this report ?
Mr. W. H. Wright, assistant chief architect.
Did the report of your own architect state what amount would be required to make good these defects that the minister has referred to ?
The report will speak for itself ; I cannot recall now whether it states any definite amount or not.
Is this $12,000 which is being asked for to pay the balance under the contract for that building ?
We have to pay for putting in the elevator yet.
Is not that included in the original contract ?
No.
Is Mr. Wright the second officer who was sent from the department ?
He is the second one and he only went a few days ago.
Who was the first gentleman to make the report ?

Mr. Dodwell, of Halifax. I may say that Mr. Dodwell sent me a confidential report. He has not had special charge of the building. Special charge of it was given to Mr. Bush. Mr. Dodwell, as resident engineer, has a general supervision of the building. He has made a confidential report on the subject. Then, I sent for Mr. Keefe and talked matters over with him after which I decided to send Mr. Wright down to make a thorough examination of the building.

The minister ought to be able to state what portion of this sum is to be devoted to the original contract. Under the minister's statement with regard to the report there is no liability on the part of the government to pay the contactor a further sum. He has failed to complete his contract and there are these serious defects which he has spoken of and which will require a considerable amount, I should think, to make them good. I think the minister ought to be able to state what portion of this sum is to be paid to the contractor.

I am unable to state what will be the result of the consideration of the report or of the negotiations, but we certainly must have some more money at once to complete the work that is absolutely essential in the building. We have to instal an elevator and that will cost several thousand dollars.
How much will the elevator cost ?
Several thousand dollars.
Then the contractor must have got all his money.

It is apparent the government has a good deal to conceal in this matter. I understood the minister to say that this building was to have been completed four years ago. That four years, I assume, have been occupied in correspondence between the government and the ar-

chitect, or the person to whom the contract was first given. I asked the question a short time ago what were the defects in construction pointed out by the government to the architect as the reason why the balance of the contract price was withheld. The minister did not answer that question but contented himself with making some remarks upon the statement of my hon. friend from Peel. I would like an answer to that question.

The report which I have just received is a confidential report from Mr. Dodwell. That being a confidential report I could not give the details of it to the contractor, but I told him that I had been informed that there were a number of important defects in the construction of the building.

What were these defects ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'.	I told him they were
important defets.	I did not enter into
the details, but I said that I would send an arctitect from the department down to Halifax and would give him an opportunity of going over the building with the architect so that he would have the most complete fair play as I did not want to do the contractor any injustice. It is just a" few days ago that the report was presented to me. Now, my intention is to have a copy of the report sent to the contractor and also to Mr. Bush. I would be very glad indeed if the Public Accounts Committee would find it convenient to take up these matters. That is the place where they should be inquired into. All the correspondence would be submitted to the committee. That would be much more convenient than attempting to consider the correspondence before a committee of the House.
The minister says there has been a report ?
Yes.

It is a report in regard to the public business and I fail to see how that would be confidential as regards this House. I think we have a right to know what the report contains. The minister says that he is about to send a copy of the report to the contractor.
I am speaking of Mr. Wright's report; it is not confidential.

In what sense could a report on a public work be confidential ? I think this committee has the right to know
the contents of that report.

That will be a matter in the judgment of the Public Accounts Committee. I am rather inclined to think that the Committee on Public Accounts would say that if an official of the depart-Mr. ALCORN.
ment who was not specially charged with the supervision of this building wrote a confidential report, it should not be produced. Personally I have no objection, but we must respect the confidence of this gentleman. I have, myself, the utmost confidence in the report of Mr. Wright, and I think that the committee, having regard to his high standing as an architect, would also have confidence in his report. That report would be submitted to the Public Accounts Committee.

I am sure that my hon. friend has every possible confidence in Mr. Dodwell, and if it had not been for that gentleman, it is probable that we might never have heard anything about that building, and we would have paid the full amount the contract calls for. It is difficult to know whether this report should be disclosed if it is confidential. The public owe a great deal to Mr. Dodwell for having first found out these conditions and having been the cause of saving the money of the country. But, there is a great deal of difference between the report of Mr. Dodwell, who is not interested, and who has had no communication with the contractor, and the report of Mr. Wright, who may be a first-class architect, but who goes down there, meets the contractor, and we can see immediately the work of the contractor, because the report of Mr. Wright does not deal at all with the information given by Mr. Dodwell. It is a question whether it would not be a good thing to have the report of Mr. Dodwell, so that we could compare the two reports.
There is no justifiable reason why it should be private. It deals with the expenditure of public money, and therefore this House is entitled to it.

It was not at my suggestion that it was marked confidential. I received this communication from Mr. Dodwell, who I presume felt it to be his duty, as an official of the government, though not specially charged with looking after this building, to give me certain information, and it is for the Public Accounts Committee to say whether that should be produced.

I think the minister should have said that as this was a public work, the report had no right to be marked confidential, and this House is entitled to see that or any other report made in connection with it.

This committee is now asked to vote this large sum to complete this building, and it appears that two reports have been made on certain defects in the building. I am quite unable to see in what sense, as regards this committee or parliament, either of these reports can be said to be confidential. It is a new doc* trine to me that parliament can be denied

information simply because some outside party chooses to mark a paper as confidential. It is for the minister to say whether information so conveyed to him is confidential as between him and parliament. Was this report so marked paid for ?
No.
The other report was paid for, I presume ?
It was made by an official of the department, whose expenses of course were paid, but there was no other charge.
That report ought to be here.

It'seems to me that the proper course would be, if it is thought desirable in the public interest that the matter should be investigated, for the Public Accounts Committee to take it up. That committee would have power to summon Mr. 1 lodwell and Mr. Bush to give evidence under oath, which of course could not be presented to this committee.
Suppose the majority of the committee refused to subpoena Mr. Dodwell.
I cannot conceive such a thing possible. I am sure the committee would be most willing to investigate this matter, as I have noticed every desire on its part to investigate every public matter.
The item then should be allowed to stand until it is investigated ; because after the money is voted, the government need not care.

The purpose of this vote will be to pay for the electric elevator and certain blinds and fittings which are necessary to put the building in shape so that it can be used by the customs authorities. I may say that there will be no money paid either to Mr. Keefe or Mr. Bush until the Committee on Public Accounts have a reasonable time to take the matter up; but we want to complete the furnishing and pay for the elevator.

The hon. minister admits that this item, at all events a part of it, is necessary for examination by the Public Accounts Committee. In that state of affairs it seems highly improper to pass the item here.

Is it necessary to make a search of title in Nova Scotia ? Is it different from Ontario, where you can go to the Registry Office and the registrar will make an abstract of title [DOT]

Yes, it is different. In some of the counties of Ontario, they have adopted what is called the Torrens system, and under that system it is not necessary to search titles as is done in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. In these provinces it is necessary to search back to the original title.

In Ontario the registrar does that where the Torrens system is not in vogue. I have had a great deal to do with the examination of titles. I send to the registrar for an abstract of title which will cost $2, $3 or $4. The lawyer looks that over and for that and comparing the deed $10 is an outside price-it costs only $5 in many cases. I am agent for one of the largest loan companies in the country and have paid $10 for this service in connection with many mortgages-never more than $20. Yet here is $79 paid to a lawyer to go into a registry office, pass a title and draw a deed. This is simply throwing away the people's money for the benefit of political favourites.

In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick no prudent man will buy a property or take a mortgage without having a solicitor examine the title. I certainly should feel that the government had been derelict in its duty if it did not employ a solicitor to make a thorough and careful search of title.
But the registrar furnishes the abstract, and he is responsible if he makes a mistake.
That is not the law with us.

I wish we had some system like that in New Brunswick. I can assure my hon. friend that when he goes to the maritime provinces, he will not get any title searched for $2 ; I advise him not to ask a registrar down there to give him an abstract of title, or at least not to purchase on such an abstract. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, titles will run back 100 years ; the original grant may have been divided and subdivided a hundred times, and there may have been a dozen conveyances. There is no such thing as a Torrens system in the maritime provinces.
There is a statute of limitations and there is no necessity to go back 100 years.

You might have to go back 40 years or even 60. As to getting an abstract of title from the registrar it is not his business to prepare an abstract and he may not know if it is a correct one or not. It is his business to register
the deeds, &e., and he might not know if the copy of an abstract was correct. What would the hon. member think of a minister who would take a conveyance with an imperfect title ? My hon. friend would be the first man to find fault. If it were simply the searching of an ordinary title, if there were no complications and there was a continuous chain from the Crown to the present owner, probably $76 would be a good fee, but I have no doubt there are complications, the property may have been sold and resold, and I am sure there is not a lawyer in this House who would not say it would be unwise for any person to buy a property without a thorough search of the title. In my own experience recently I found a mortgage 20 years old that was undischarged and the parties concerned dead, so that I had to get administration to have the thing cleared up.
I will not state that I would charge $76 to search a title, but this charge is not stated to be for the searching of a title ; it is for legal services ; that includes many things besides searching titles.
