These things do not appeal to the public. I see the Minister of Railways present and that recalls to my recollection the fact that in the last election held in Centre York, there

was a meeting in the village of Markham at which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) showed the plans and specifications of a new building which the government were going to put up there. But in spite of this appeal of the ministers, the people there actually went back on the government by some thirty votes.
That shows how self-sacrificing we are to give these public buildings where they do not affect the vote.

But the ministers are not self-sacrificing at their own expense. This is done for the purpose of parading the public money before the people and get-ing them to vote for the government because of the local expenditure in these places.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is your side who are taking up the time.
If the hon. gentleman will look into the matter, he will find that more time has been taken up by members supporting the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on the estimates.
It lias been taken up by the ministers and their supporters more than by the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Has not three-fourths of the speaking to-day been on the side of my hon. friend ?
The minister occupied fullv one-half the time himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He has to answer questions.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the plans were exhibited at that meeting ?
Yes.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken.

I can get the report in the newspapers of that meeting. Senator Campbell was present and announced that he had the plans and that the building would be a magnificent one, and he gave that as an earnest of what they could do.
Does my hon. friend say that the cost of maintaining each of these buildings is $2,500 per year ?

I find it would run to about $2,000 a year. Some of them run to more than that. The building at Bridgewater cost some $40,000. It is time that these huge expenditures should be stopped. If the same amount of money had been invested a few years ago in transportation, the country would have had some benefit. There is a list that will startle the average man throughout the Dominion. All that money is sacrificed simply out of a desire to gain political advantage. What necessity is there in a village like Markham with some 967 people, for a public building where formerly they had good post office accommodation at a total cost of $00 per year. But the country has to launch into a large public building, to maintain which it will cost $2,000 per year. It is high time that a protest should be made against spending money in this ridiculous way in these small places.
I think we ought now to rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the rate we are going, it will take a good many days yet to go through the estimates.

That is not our fault.
St. John, New Brunswick, Dominion buildings-improvements, repairs, &c., $4,000.
This is for repairs to the custom house, post office, &c.
Is that done by day's labour or by contract ?
The amounts are all small ones and the work is done by day's labour.
Is there an inspector on works of that kind ?

We have the superintendent of buildings there.
St. John military building-addition to stores building and wagon and gun shed, $6,000.
What is this estimated to cost?
The estimate is $33,044.93.
Was there a contract in this case?

Yes, after public advertisement.
Mr. FOWLER, How much more will be required to complete.it?
St. John quarantine station, Partridge island-to complete water service, &c., $2,500.
How much has been paid on account of that water service? It seems to me we have had a vote for that every year.
This $2,500 is to complete the work. I made a statement concerning it on a former occasion. The total probable cost is $54,988.91.
Are you boring?

No. There is a water pipe laid from the mainland. A trench had

to be excavated and the pipe laid. There was an accident to the pipe which added to the expense. The hon. member for the city of St. John (Mr. Daniel) is familiar with the case.
Is this under contract?
It is done under the direction of the resident engineer. It is to give a fresh-water supply to Partridge Island.

Does the hon. minister intend to have an item for a public building at Hillsborough in the supplementary estimates?
Mr. PUGSLEYL If it is decided to erect a public building at Hillsborough to which I have been urged very strongly by Hon. Mr. Osman more especially, as "well as by some other residents there, of course, it will appear in the supplementary estimates.
Mr. CROCKET, been going on ?

Mr. FOWLER, artesian well?
How long has the work Since 1904.
Did they try boring an

Yes, and struck salt water at a great depth.
St. John quarantine station, Partridge island-site for steam sterilizer; dwelling for boatman: improvement and repair to existing buildings, &c., $5,000.
This is to provide a steam sterilizer and also a cottage- for the orderly. This is asked for by the director general of public health, Dr. Montizambert
Does not the government own Partridge Island? Why then do they need to procure a site for the steam sterilizer?

This is needed merely to provide the site-to build up the walls to make a level site for the building. This is a rocky island and the site for the building must be prepared.
Tracadie lazaretto-laundry and sanitary works, $6,OCO.
This is the lazaretto where lepers are taken care of. It is in Gloucester county. This money is to provide a laundry and septic tank.
How many lepers are there now ?
I believe there are thirteen. This is a wonderfully well conducted institution, and deserving of being very carefully looked after.
Does' the minister know if the lepers are decreasing or not?
As a representative of the district, I have for a number of years urged the erection of a public building there.
I have not heard from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) on the subject.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) has not been Minister of Public Works all the time.
What is the population of Hillsborough ?
Greater than that of most of the places where these buildings have been provided. This building would serve between 3,000 and 4,000 people.

A very prominent and influential citizen (Hon. Mr. Osman), called upon me in addition to corresponding upon the subject, and said that if the government would erect a building there, the company with which he was connected would give the site free. He urged very strongly favourable consideration of the matter. I have said that, as minister, I was disposed to take a very favourable view of the case, recognizing that it was desirable to give to the people the necessary accommodation. For I do not take the view taken by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) on this subject. Judging from the complacency with which my hon. friend from King's and Albert (Mr. Fowler) listened to that hon. gentleman, I thought that he coincided with his views. It came to me as a matter of surprise that my hon. friend should urge the providing of a building for Hillsboro. Another* reason for my surprise was that, though I have been minister since August last, I have not had the pleasure of receiving any communication, written or verbal, from the hon. gentleman on the subject.
My hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) could probably tell the committee better than I.
The number is decreasing so far as the locality is concerned. But Dr. Smith, the surgeon of the hospital, was sent to the west a month or so ago to bring in another case.
Are these all the items for New Brunswick?
Yes.

The hon. minister speaks of the complacency with which I regarded the remarks of the hon. member for East Simcoe. I was merely copying the complacency of the hon. minister himself, and surely he does not object to hon. members. modelling themselves on his pattern. I have urged the construction of a public building at Hillsborough every session since I first had the honour of representing the county of Albert. With respect to providing buildings in these small towns, it seems to be a principle adopted by this govern-

ment. That being the case, I fail to see why a place of the importance of Hillsborough should not be recognized, since it is far more important than the great majority of the places that have already received public buildings. There Is a considerable revenue in Hillsborough, there is a custom house, it is a customs sub-port, and a post office would accommodate a very large number of people, both in the village and in the surrounding country. Among all the places that have been favoured this year there is not a solitary place with better claims for a public building than Hillsborough. I do not know what the minister's reason was for trying to make out that I had not been doing my duty by making a request for the erection of this building. If it was with the desire to injure me with my constituents his policy will entirely fail, because my constituents in that portion of the district I represent are fully aware of the fact that I have repeatedly urged upon the government the erection of this building. I think the Finance Minister at one time was acting Minister of Public Works, and he as good as promised me that this town would receive proper consideration. I am glad that his promise is likely to be carried out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not remember the promise, but on general principles I am in favour of erecting these buildings. I only make this request, that when the speech of the hon. member for East Simcoe about the terrible expense of these buildings, is distributed, as I have no doubt it will be widely distributed, I think the hon. member for King's and Albert (Mr. Fowler) ought to arrange that his very effective reply should go with it.

My hon. friend from King's and Albert takes this ground, and I take the same ground, that if the government is going to throw thousands of money away indiscriminately, then the most deserving places should be first regarded.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a change of ground. My hon. friend stated solemnly that it is time this.expenditure was stopped ; that is a solemn duty he imposes upon us. I do not agree with him. He warns us that we must not do it any longer ; then the hon. member for Kings and Albert gets up and says, don't mind my hon. friend from Simcoe but give us ta building in Hillsborough.

It will be a good idea for the hon. member for Simcoe to pick out all these places like Hillsborough, Markham, Pictou, Acton vale, and a number of other small towns in Ontario and Quebec, and move a resolution that it is against public policy and against public interest that public buildings should be erected in these places. That would be a courageous and manly
course to take. Let him try that and see where he will be.

The Minister of Public Works was not in the House a few years ago when we spent a whole night discussing an appropriation for the little town of Dunnville. The opposition then declared that no public buildings should be erected in small places unless they were justified by tlie population and the post office revenue.
What is the limit of population ?

I think 3,000 was the suggested limit. But here is a public building costing $25,000 in a small village of 900 or
1,000	of a population, and very little revenue ; while other towns with 3,000 or 4,000 and over are left out. There should be some system adopted. The revenue should amount to so much and the population should be so much before the government expends public money there. That was .he policy adopted by the opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And I think my hon. friend voted against the very thing he now proposes.

My hon. friend has been in parliament a good while. Now let me call his attention to what I think is just about as laudable a thing as the Conservative government ever did, and that was the erection of a public building in the thriving town of Sussex when the population I am sure was not over 800.

Oh, yes, the population then would be about 1,600.
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. Even so that would be about 1,400 less than the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says it should be.

Does the hon. gentleman think there are 1,500 people in Sussex now.
Mr. FOW'LEIi. Yes, 2,500.
It has grown a great leal in the last year, then.

The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says that the erection >f public buildings, such as custom houses, post offices and so forth, should be dependent upon the revenue derived therefrom, f may say to him that in 1896 when the Liberal party came into power, for three years I had been applying to the Minister of Railways and Canals to have a station in my village, St. Michel de Bellechasse. in election after election we had been promised this station, but as the parish judged it proper to give a majority against the rovernment then we did not get the station. Finally I came to the Minister of Railways and Canals and told him that I would like to have a station in my village.

Well, lie said, there is uo revenue, the revenue last year was only $350. I pledged myself that if a station costing $1,200 or $1,500 was built, within a year the revenue would amount to over $2,000. The station was built, and in my parish where there was then a revenue of $280, we have this year a revenue of $7,000, owing to the existence of this station.

X understood the Minister of Public Works to say that he could not subscribe to the principle that had been in vogue heretofore with regard to the erection of public buildings. I think it would be well for him to lay down what he regards as the proper principle. I have held the view for many years, while our friends were in power as well as during the last 12 years, that wherever a convenient and suitable public building can be rented at a much less amount than it would cost to pay the interest on maintenance charges for a public building, that, in the interest of the country, it is desirable that a public building should not be erected in such a place. I do not care whether the place is large or small. I would make no difference in that regard. It is not a good principle and is no evidence of economy or desire to economize when public money is spent on the erection of a public building in a small village or town of 1,000 or 15,000 inhabitants. We would have to pay for the building say $10,000; on that the interest would be about $450 per annum, the care of the building about $400, heating about $100, lighting about $75, insurance about $25, and repairs about $50 a year. That is an annual expenditure of about $1,000, when in many cases a good and suitable building can be' rented for not more than $100 to $125 a year. To that you would have to add probably $50 or $60 for fuel and light, and the people would have as good service as with a public building for which you would have to pay out $1,000 a year. Take Owen Sound for instance. A post office building is now being erected there for the first time. It is a county town of over 10,000 inhabitants, but has never had a public building up to the present time. The people asked for one occasionally but were not pushing for it, because a good building could be rented for very much less. In the adjoining town of Meaford, of about
3,000	inhabitants, they have never had a public building erected for post office, custom house or inland revenue, but have rented a building at a very moderate price. In Markdale, the village in which I live, with about 1,200 inhabitants, the rent paid for a very good post office is, I think, $125 with $60 for heating and lighting. Durham with over 3,000 has no public building. The minister is coming in as a new member of the cabinet. He is at the head of a very important spending department, and he should Mr. TALBOT.
take this into his consideration and lay down some principle, letting the House and the country know that he has made a departure upon good, safe business lines and desires to save the money of the people while giving them all the convenience they require in the matter of public buildings.

I do not think one could properly lay down a fixed rule that there should be no public building erected in a town unless it has a population of
3,000	or more.
I did not go that far because there are places where you cannot get buildings ; but I say you should rent where you can procure a suitable building.

I spoke of the public building erected in the very enterprising town of Sussex, because knowledge of it came to me as I was brought up in that locality. That building was regarded by the people as a very great improvement. It created a local pride among the people who saw this not expensive but nice building erected by the government. The county in which it is erected has not received any federal expenditure for wharfs, dredging, etc., as it is entirely inland. With an inland town where no money is expended for any purpose exeept the postal service, if you have a thriving town of only 3,000 or even 2,000, and the people feel that they would like to have a public building or some little expenditure, I do not think it is improper that their wishes should be met in that particular. Suppose we were to limit the erection of post offices and other public buildings to the larger towns the result would be very discouraging to the people who are living in smaller towns. They would see money being spent for dredging and the building of wharfs in other places and it would be discouraging to them. If money was being expended in the county for wharfs, &c., you might well say to them that for the present they should wait a little before asking for a public building. Therefore, I think it is impossible to lay down a hard and fast rule. Take the west where towns are springing up rapidly, where a town with a population of only 1,000 to-day may be full of hope and full of possibilities and the people ask a public building, is it not a reasonable encouragement to the people that a public building should be erected for post office and customs purposes ? Many applications have been made to me from the people of different towns urging that public buildings should be erected. While I would not erect buildings in towns of very small population, yet I would be very reluctant indeed to say that no public building should be erected in a place which has not more than 3,000 population or even
2,000.	Take the town of Hillsborough ; the hon. member for Kings and Albert said

that if the rule were fixed at 3,000 or even at 2,000, a public building could not be erected.
Revenue should count as well as population.

If we were to be governed entirely by revenue what would we have to do ? Take the case of Montreal ; we are asked to erect a post office building there. It is going to be very costly, it will cost nearly half a million dollars in addition to the site. A plain building, absolutely without ornamentation, a building which might suit the purpose, I suppose, might be erected for half that money. What are we expending in these cities large sums of money for ?-for the purpose of erecting buildings which are beautiful, and to which people will look with pride and pleasure. It is because we take a pride in the community and seek to move along with it and gratify the feeling of the people that this money is spent. Money which is spent for the purpose of beautifying a building, making it more comfortable and convenient for the people to transact their business in may be regarded by some people as money wasted. Yet, it is not wasted. When the government, in a small and thriving town, where the people have ho other expenditure of public money, erects a small building which is a good specimen of architecture and in which the people take pride it is doing something to help them in their efforts to advance the community residing in that locality. I am not prepared to say that it is a waste of money, or that it is something to be condemned. I am a great believer in doing what is reasonable in the various sections of the country to encourage the people living in the smaller towns to take a pride in the places in which they live, and I would not say that there should be a fixed rule as to the population of the places in which we could erect buildings or that the question of revenue should be the sole consideration.

I did not mention either of the rules that the minister talks about. He has been talking round the question for a quarter of an hour. The minister argued that it is a matter of pride with various communities that they should have public buildings in their midst. Let us apply that to domestic life. Suppose that the bon. Minister's wife has a pride and an ambition which prompts her to want a bonnet costing $100 and the minister's finances will not justify him in making the expenditure ; would he apply that principle to the expenditure of his own money ? Would he spend his own money in the same lavish way that he spends the country's money ? If he is not prepared to do with the country's money as he would do with his own he is not following the best and safest guide. Another
argument is that many of these places, being inland places do not get much expenditure and that they are entitled to public buildings. I presume that the expenditure of money in these places helps to carry elections. If that be a sound principle then I say let us divide the money up equitably among all these places.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is socialism.

No, it is not socialistic at all. The Minister of Finance is just a little too previous.
If it is fair and proper that because these constituencies have no general expenditure within their bounds they should have public buildings, then I say they are .entitled to their full share just as wrell as others. They have a perfect right to claim it and it is due to them that they should get it. If the minister follows out that principle I do not see how he can refuse it to all. He says we cannot follow any hard and fast rule. I did not ask that any hard and fast rule be followed. He says that we cannot regard a mere fixed population. I did not ask that a mere fixed population be regarded, whether it is 3.000, 4,000 5,000 or 10,000. I pointed to a town of 12,000 where there is no post office yet and another or 3,000 and smaller places along the line. I did not name a fixed population but I did lay down this rule that whether a place is large or small, if a public building can be secured in a central locality for the needs of the people at a smaller amount of money than that which would be required to pay the interest on the money that would be put into the erection of a public building, caretaking, heating, and maintenance, I did not see any justification for spending more money to supply the needs of the people in any place when we could supply the needs of the people for less money.
You put it down to the bare question of dollars and cents ?

I put it down to the principle of saving the peoples' money. If you can give the people the conveniences that they require for less money by renting a building than erecting a building, then I would rent a building. There are some places where you cannot rent a building. I can understand that in many places in the west you could not rent a building and under those circumstances the government would be justified in erecting a building. When you cannot rent and provide the people with the conveniences they require go on and build, but if you can rent a suitable building for less money than it costs to erect a building I do not understand by what principle of economy you would be justified iu expending a larger amount.
